q: Frank buys bananas (x) and oranges (y). His budget line changes from y=30−2x to y=20−x. A possible explanation?
explain: Vertical intercept m/py falls 30 to 20 and slope size px/py falls 2 to 1. Holding px fixed, py must rise (slope px/py halves) and m must rise (old 30·py = 15·px is below new 20·py = 20·px), so oranges' price and income both increased.
a: The price of oranges and Frank's income both increased.

q: Willy: football 20 + Fortnite 30 is as good as football 50 + Fortnite 10; preferences convex. He now plays Fortnite 20 min. Minimum football time to be at least as well off? (convex ⇒ chord)
explain: With convex preferences the chord joining two indifferent bundles is at least as good; the midpoint of (football 20, Fortnite 30) and (football 50, Fortnite 10) is (35, 20), so at Fortnite 20 he needs football 35.

q: Peter's indifference curves: y = k/x − 2 (higher k is better). Peter strictly prefers (5,8) to which of (8,5), (9,4), (6,7)?
explain: Write k=(y+2)x: (5,8) gives 50 while (8,5) gives 56, (9,4) gives 54 and (6,7) gives 54; every alternative has a higher k, so Peter prefers none of them to (5,8).
a: None of these bundles. [k=(y+2)x: (5,8)→50, but (8,5)→56, (9,4)→54, (6,7)→54, all higher, so he prefers none of them.]

q: Rachel consumes 5 packs blackberries + 6 oats, p(black)=2·p(oats). Income doubles, p(oats) doubles, p(black) unchanged. If she still buys 6 oats, max blackberry packs? (let p(oats)=1)
explain: Let p(oats)=1 so p(black)=2 and initial income = 5·2 + 6·1 = 16; after income doubles to 32 with p(oats)=2, oats cost 6·2 = 12, leaving 20 for blackberries at price 2, i.e. 10 packs.

q: Elis loves sport most, also likes reading; reading on the horizontal axis, sport on the vertical. Her indifference curves are likely:
explain: Sport (vertical) is her favourite, so she sacrifices little sport for extra reading (horizontal); the MRS is small in size, giving relatively flat indifference curves (slope below 1 in absolute value).
a: Flatter — slope below 1 in absolute value (she gives up little sport for reading).

q: Juliet has 400 for milk (25/bottle) and cereal. Cereal is 60 for the first 2 packs, then 80 each. She buys 3 cereal packs. How many milk bottles can she afford?
explain: Three cereal packs cost 60 + 60 + 80 = 200 (60 each for the first two, 80 for the third), leaving 400 minus 200 = 200 for milk at 25 each, i.e. 8 bottles.

q: Which is true? weakly vs strictly monotonic and neutral goods.
explain: Strict monotonicity means more of any good is strictly preferred, so no good can be neutral; only weak monotonicity permits a neutral good.
a: If preferences are strictly monotonic, a good can never be neutral. [weak monotonicity still allows a neutral good.]

q: Tony: px doubles and py triples, income fixed. On the (x horizontal, y vertical) graph the new budget line is:
explain: New slope size (2·px)/(3·py) = (2/3)·(px/py) is smaller, so the line is flatter; both intercepts m/(2·px) and m/(3·py) shrink, so it lies inside the old line.
a: Flatter and lies below the old budget line.

q: Garry: perfect complements, 2 donuts per 1 coffee (never one without the other). Coffee horizontal, donuts vertical. Slope of the indifference curve at (2 coffees, 2 donuts)?
explain: With 2 donuts per coffee the kink needs donuts = 2·coffee; at (2 coffees, 2 donuts) donuts are scarce and coffee is in excess, so the point sits on the horizontal arm and the indifference-curve slope is 0.

q: Eve spends all income on avocados and walnuts. She can just afford (9 avocados, 10 walnuts) or (3, 12). One avocado costs 20. Her weekly income?
explain: Both bundles lie on the budget line: 9·20 + 10·pw = 3·20 + 12·pw gives pw = 60, so income = 9·20 + 10·60 = 780.

q: Elis: u(x,y)=3x(y<sup>0.5</sup>+2), at (2,4). Marginal utility of x? [MU<sub>x</sub>=3(y<sup>0.5</sup>+2)=3(2+2)=12]
explain: MU_x = du/dx = 3(y^0.5 + 2); at y=4 that is 3(2+2) = 12 (it does not depend on x here).

q: Henry: u(x,y)=(x+3)(y<sup>0.5</sup>+2), at (3,4). If y drops to 0, what x keeps him exactly as well off? [set (x+3)(0+2)=(6)(4)]
explain: Current utility (3+3)(4^0.5 + 2) = 6·4 = 24; with y=0 utility is (x+3)·2, so set 2(x+3) = 24, giving x+3 = 12 and x = 9.

q: u(x,y)=x<sup>0.7</sup>y<sup>0.3</sup> at (3,7), x horizontal. The absolute value of MRS<sub>yx</sub> is:
explain: Absolute MRS = (0.7/0.3)(y/x) = (7/3)(7/3) = 49/9 which is about 5.4, so it exceeds 1.

q: Willy always consumes 2 units of x with 3 units of y. A utility function representing his preferences could be:
explain: u=min(6x,4y) kinks where 6x = 4y, i.e. y = 1.5·x, which is 3 units of y for every 2 units of x, matching his fixed 2-with-3 ratio.
a: u=min(6x,4y) — kink at 6x=4y ⇒ y=(3/2)x, i.e. 2x with 3y. (Any positive transform such as 4·min(6x,4y) also works.)

q: Jill burns 300 cal per hour walking (w) and 500 cal per hour skiing (s), and wants to maximise calories. Her utility function might be:
explain: Calories are perfect substitutes; 300w + 500s, or any positive multiple such as 6w + 10s (ratio 300:500 = 6:10 = 3:5), represents maximising calories.
a: u(w,s)=6w+10s (perfect substitutes in the ratio of calories, 300:500 = 6:10).

q: Henry: U(x1,x2)=x1 + x2<sup>0.5</sup>. His indifference curves are:
explain: u = x1 + sqrt(x2) is quasilinear in x1; solving x1 = U minus sqrt(x2) gives a downward slope minus 1/(2·sqrt(x2)) and positive curvature, so the curves are downward-sloping and convex.
a: Downward-sloping, convex curves (quasilinear in x1).

q: Two goods with always-positive marginal utilities and convex preferences. Then:
explain: Perfect complements have flat and vertical segments where extra units of the abundant good add zero marginal utility; strictly positive MU everywhere is incompatible, so they cannot be perfect complements.
a: These two goods cannot be perfect complements. [positive MU everywhere rules out the flat/vertical arms of an L-shape.]

q: Which is true? strictly monotonic and perfect complements.
explain: On the arms of an L-shaped (complements) map, more of one good leaves utility unchanged, which violates strict monotonicity; hence strict monotonicity rules out perfect complements.
a: If preferences are strictly monotonic, goods can never be perfect complements.

q: Which statement about the MRS is correct?
explain: Strict convexity forces a strictly diminishing MRS; ordinary (weak) convexity permits a constant MRS (perfect substitutes), so only the strict-convexity statement is correct.
a: Whenever preferences are STRICTLY convex, the MRS must be diminishing along the indifference curve. [plain convexity allows a constant MRS.]

q: Jake: perfect complements, 2 donuts per 1 coffee. Donuts horizontal, coffee vertical. Slope of the indifference curve at (5 donuts, 2 coffees)?
explain: The kink needs donuts = 2·coffee; at (5 donuts, 2 coffees) only 4 donuts are needed, so donuts are in excess on the horizontal arm and the slope is 0.

q: Luke: u(x,y)=x(y+1), income 30, demands 5 units of x and 1 unit of y. Price of y? [tangency + budget]
explain: Tangency (y+1)/x = px/py at (5,1) gives px/py = 2/5; the budget 5·px + py = 30 with px = (2/5)·py gives 3·py = 30, so py = 10.

q: Susan: u=min(4x,3y), income 30, px=2, consumes 3 units of x. Price of y? [kink 4x=3y ⇒ y=4; 2·3+py·4=30]
explain: The complements kink 4x = 3y with x=3 gives y=4; the budget 2·3 + py·4 = 30 gives py = 6.

q: Consumer's optimum has MU_beef/MU_pork > p_beef/p_pork. Then she must:
explain: MU_beef/MU_pork greater than p_beef/p_pork rearranges to MU_beef/p_beef greater than MU_pork/p_pork; the last crown spent on beef beats pork everywhere, so the optimum is a corner with beef only.
a: Be consuming beef but no pork (corner: the last crown on beef beats pork).

q: Rachel: u=4x+2y (coffee x, tea y), px=3, py=1, income 12. Cups of tea? [MU per crown: tea 2/1=2 vs coffee 4/3≈1.33 ⇒ all on tea]
explain: Perfect substitutes: compare marginal utility per crown, coffee 4/3 (about 1.33) against tea 2/1 = 2; tea yields more utility per crown, so she spends all 12 on tea, giving 12 cups.

q: Fanta & Mirinda are one-for-one perfect substitutes. He bought 15 Fanta and 0 Mirinda. Which statement MUST be false?
explain: Buying only Fanta among one-for-one substitutes needs Fanta to be weakly cheaper (equal marginal utilities), so 'Fanta is more expensive than Mirinda' must be false.
a: Fanta is more expensive than Mirinda. [buying only Fanta needs Fanta weakly cheaper, so 'Fanta more expensive' is impossible.]

q: In-kind vs cash transfer: when is the consumer as well off with cash as with an in-kind transfer of equal value?
explain: Cash weakly dominates an in-kind grant; they are equivalent only when the in-kind constraint does not bind, that is when she would already buy at least that much of the good.
a: If she usually consumes plenty of that good in her optimum (the in-kind constraint does not bind).

q: Susan: p_ham=6, p_cheese=8, MU_ham=10, MU_cheese=7. Then:
explain: MU per crown is 10/6 (about 1.67) for ham against 7/8 (about 0.88) for cheese; since ham gives more utility per crown, shifting spending toward ham raises utility.
a: Without changing spending she could raise utility by consuming more ham and less cheese. [MU/p: 10/6 > 7/8.]

q: Jim treats car-rental days and gasoline as perfect complements (3 gallons/day). The car-rental price doubles; other prices and the budget unchanged. Which is TRUE?
explain: With gasoline and days in a fixed 3-to-1 ratio, both fall in the same proportion; days = m/(r+3g) becomes m/(2r+3g), and (r+3g)/(2r+3g) exceeds 1/2, so each falls by less than 50%.
a: His gasoline use and rental days both fall by LESS than 50%.

q: Peter: continuous, strictly convex, monotonic preferences, but a NON-convex budget set. Which statement is FALSE?
explain: With a non-convex budget set a tangency (MRS = budget slope) can be only a local optimum, so 'a tangency must be an optimum' is the false statement.
a: 'If a bundle satisfies MRS = budget slope, it must be an optimum.' [with a non-convex budget the tangency can be a local, not global, best — so this is false.]

q: A consumer has income 40, px=4, py=2. If she spends everything on good x, how many units can she buy (the x-intercept of the budget line)?
explain: The x-intercept is m/px = 40/4 = 10 units.

q: With px=3 and py=6 (good x on the horizontal axis), the slope of the budget line is:
explain: The budget-line slope is minus px/py = minus 3/6 = minus 1/2.

q: A shop gives a uniform 50 percent discount on every good. The budget line:
explain: Cutting every price by the same proportion is like raising real income: the line shifts outward parallel with no kink.
opts: shifts outward parallel to the old one, with no kink
develops a kink at the discount point

q: Income rises from 60 to 90 with both prices unchanged. The budget line:
explain: A pure income change leaves the price ratio (slope) fixed, so the line shifts outward parallel.
opts: shifts outward parallel to the old one

q: The vertical intercept (on the good-y axis) of the budget line px·x + py·y = m equals:
explain: Setting x=0 gives py·y = m, so the vertical intercept is m/py.

q: The budget-line slope minus px/py represents:
explain: The slope minus px/py is the market rate of exchange: how many units of y must be given up to buy one more x.
opts: the market rate at which x can be traded for y

q: At an interior (tangency) optimum, the marginal rate of substitution equals:
explain: The tangency condition sets the MRS equal to the price ratio px/py.

q: For Cobb-Douglas utility u = xᵃyᵇ, the share of income spent on good x is:
explain: Cobb-Douglas demand gives a constant expenditure share of a/(a+b) on good x.

q: For u = xᵃyᵇ the Marshallian demand x* = (a/(a+b))·m/px depends on:
explain: The Cobb-Douglas demand for x involves only income and its own price; py cancels out.

q: For perfect substitutes u = ax + by, the consumer buys only good x when:
explain: Spend where marginal utility per crown is highest; only x is bought when a/px exceeds b/py.

q: For perfect complements u = min(x, y), the optimum always lies where:
explain: The L-shaped map has its kink on the ray x = y, where neither good is wasted.

q: When income rises and prices are fixed, the demand for a normal good:
explain: A normal good is defined by demand that rises with income.

q: When income rises and prices are fixed, the demand for an inferior good:
explain: An inferior good is defined by demand that falls as income rises.

q: Bruno's owner has 24 crowns for biscuits (px=3) and chews. Spending all of it on biscuits, how many biscuits can she buy?
explain: The biscuit intercept is 24/3 = 8 biscuits.

q: The horizontal intercept (on the good-x axis) of the budget line equals:
explain: Setting y=0 gives px·x = m, so the horizontal intercept is m/px.

q: For perfect substitutes u = ax + by, the optimum is generally:
explain: Straight-line indifference curves give a corner solution unless px/py exactly equals a/b.
opts: a corner, unless the price ratio equals the MRS

q: A consumer is equally well off with cash as with an in-kind gift of the same value when:
explain: Cash weakly dominates; the two coincide only when the in-kind constraint does not bind.
opts: she would have bought at least that much of the good anyway

q: If px rises while py and income stay fixed, the budget line:
explain: The y-intercept m/py is unchanged, the x-intercept m/px shrinks, so the line pivots inward and steepens.
opts: pivots inward about the y-intercept and becomes steeper

q: For Cobb-Douglas u = xᵃyᵇ, doubling income (prices fixed) changes the demand for x so that:
explain: Cobb-Douglas demand x* = (a/(a+b))·m/px is proportional to income, so doubling m doubles x (income elasticity 1).

q: If px falls while py and income stay fixed, the budget line becomes:
explain: A lower px raises the x-intercept while the y-intercept is fixed, so the line pivots outward and flattens.
opts: flatter, pivoting outward about the y-intercept

q: For Bruno, hockey minutes and football minutes are one-for-one perfect substitutes (u = h + f), and hockey is cheaper. He spends:
explain: With identical marginal utilities he buys only the cheaper good, hockey.

q: u = xy with income 40, px=2, py=4. The optimal quantity of x is:
explain: Cobb-Douglas with equal exponents: x* = (1/2)·m/px = (1/2)·40/2 = 10.

q: u = xy with income 40, px=2, py=4. The optimal quantity of y is:
u = x^0.5·y^0.5, income 100, px=5. The optimal quantity of x is:
explain: Equal exponents give x* = (1/2)·m/px = (1/2)·100/5 = 10.

q: u = x^0.3·y^0.7, income 60, px=3. The optimal quantity of x is:
u = x^0.4·y^0.6, income 200. Total spending on good y is:
explain: The y-share is 0.6, so spending on y is 0.6·200 = 120.

q: u = 2x + 3y (perfect substitutes), px=2, py=2, income 12. The optimal quantity of y is:
explain: Marginal utility per crown is 2/2 = 1 for x and 3/2 = 1.5 for y, so all income goes to y: 12/2 = 6.

q: u = x + y (one-for-one substitutes), px=3, py=4, income 24. The optimal quantity of x is:
explain: With equal marginal utilities he buys only the cheaper good x: 24/3 = 8.

q: u = min(x, y), px=2, py=3, income 25. The optimal quantity of x is:
explain: On the ray x = y the budget is (px+py)·x = m, so x = 25/(2+3) = 5.

q: u = min(2x, y) so the optimum needs y = 2x. With px=3, py=1, income 20, the optimal quantity of x is:
explain: Substitute y = 2x into the budget: 3x + 1·2x = 5x = 20, so x = 4.

q: Income is 100 and py is fixed. If px rises from 5 to 10, the x-intercept of the budget line becomes:
explain: The x-intercept is m/px = 100/10 = 10 (down from 100/5 = 20).

q: Income and px both double while py is fixed. The maximum affordable quantity of x:
explain: The x-intercept m/px becomes (2m)/(2px) = m/px, so it is unchanged.

q: For Bruno one beef treat is worth two chicken treats (u = 2·beef + chicken). Beef costs 3, chicken 2. He buys:
explain: Marginal utility per crown is 2/3 (about 0.67) for beef and 1/2 for chicken, so beef wins: only beef.

q: u = min(x, y), income 20, py=1. If px rises from 3 to 7, the optimal quantity of x changes from 5 to:
explain: On x = y the demand is x = m/(px+py) = 20/(7+1) = 2.5.

q: u = x^0.7·y^0.3 at the bundle (x=4, y=2). The absolute value of the MRS of x for y is:
u = x^(1/3)·y^(2/3), income 90, px=2. The optimal quantity of x is:
Film tickets f and streaming s give u = f^0.25·s^0.75. Income 48, price of a film ticket 4. The optimal number of film tickets is:
A consumer just exhausts income on either (12 units x, 3 units y) or (6 units x, 9 units y). If py=2, then px equals:
explain: Both bundles cost the same: 12·px + 3·2 = 6·px + 9·2, so 6·px = 12 and px = 2.

q: A consumer just exhausts income on either (9 units x, 2 units y) or (3 units x, 6 units y). If px=2, her income is:
explain: From 9·2 + 2·py = 3·2 + 6·py we get py = 3, so income = 9·2 + 2·3 = 24.

q: u = x²·y (so a=2, b=1), income 90, px=6. The optimal quantity of x is:
For u = 4x + 2y the consumer is willing to hold both goods (an interior optimum) only if px/py equals:
explain: Interior optima for perfect substitutes require the price ratio to equal the MRS a/b = 4/2 = 2.

q: For perfect complements u = min(3x, 4y) with px=2 and py=1, the own-price elasticity of demand for good y is:
explain: Demand y = m/((4/3)px + py); its own-price elasticity is minus 3py/(4px+3py) = minus 3/11 at px=2, py=1.

q: For perfect complements the two goods are always consumed together. Hence the cross-price elasticity of x with respect to py and the own-price elasticity of y are:
explain: Because x and y move in lockstep (fixed ratio), the percentage change in x equals that in y for any price change, so the two elasticities coincide.
opts: equal in size but opposite in sign

q: Demand is x = 0.04m minus 0.5·px. At m=1000 and px=20, the quantity demanded is:
Demand is x = 0.04m minus 0.5·px, giving x = 30 at m=1000, px=20. The income elasticity of demand is:
explain: Income elasticity = (dx/dm)(m/x) = 0.04·(1000/30) = 4/3 (a luxury at this point).

q: For the demand x = 0.04m minus 0.5·px, good x is:
explain: The income coefficient dx/dm = 0.04 is positive, so demand rises with income and x is normal.
opts: normal, because demand rises with income
inferior, because demand falls with income

q: u = min(2x, 5y) so the optimum needs 2x = 5y. With px=4, py=3, income 26, the optimal quantity of x is:
explain: Substitute y = (2/5)x into the budget: 4x + 3·(2/5)x = 5.2x = 26, so x = 5 (and y = 2).

q: u = x²·y³ (so a=2, b=3), income 100. Total spending on good x is:
explain: The x-share is a/(a+b) = 2/5, so spending on x is (2/5)·100 = 40.

q: u = (x+2)(y^0.5 + 1) at the bundle (x=2, y=9). If y falls to 0, the quantity of x that keeps utility unchanged is:
explain: Current utility is (2+2)(3+1) = 16; with y=0 it is (x+2)·1, so x + 2 = 16 gives x = 14.

q: u = xy, px=2, py=5, income 60. At the optimum the MRS y/x equals px/py. The optimal quantity of x is:
explain: Equal-exponent Cobb-Douglas: x* = (1/2)·m/px = (1/2)·60/2 = 15 (then y = 6, and y/x = 6/15 = 2/5 = px/py).

q: For perfect complements u = min(3x, 4y) with px=2 and py=1, the own-price elasticity of demand for good x is:
explain: Demand x = m/(px + (3/4)py); its own-price elasticity is minus 4px/(4px+3py) = minus 8/11 at px=2, py=1.

q: Strict monotonicity implies indifference curves are:
explain: Strong (strict) monotonicity means adding to even one good strictly improves the bundle, so indifference curves can have no flat or vertical segment and must slope strictly downward.

q: Which assumption guarantees that two indifference curves never cross?
explain: Transitivity (A≽B and B≽C ⇒ A≽C) prevents indifference curves from crossing; a crossing would force one bundle to be both strictly better than and indifferent to another.

q: “A balanced mix is at least as good as either extreme” describes:
explain: Convexity is the axiom that a balanced mix (average) of two bundles is at least as good as either extreme.

q: A diminishing MRS (in absolute value) as you move right is a consequence of strict:
explain: A diminishing MRS (curves bowed toward the origin) follows from strict convexity of preferences, not from monotonicity or the rationality axioms.

q: Perfect-complement (Leontief) preferences violate strict:
explain: Perfect complements min(x,y) fail STRONG monotonicity: at x=y, adding only the abundant good leaves the min (and utility) unchanged, so 'more of one good' is not strictly better. They remain continuous, transitive and complete. (Original distractor 'convexity' was replaced: Leontief also fails strict convexity, which made two options correct.)

q: Which assumption ensures that an indifference curve passes through every bundle?
explain: Completeness — every pair of bundles can be ranked — guarantees every bundle is assigned to an indifference set, so an indifference curve passes through each bundle.

q: Bill finds C₁∼C₂∼C₃∼C₄∼C₅∼C₆ pairwise, yet strictly prefers C₁ to C₆. This violates:
explain: Chaining the indifferences C₁∼C₂∼…∼C₆ must give C₁∼C₆ by transitivity; a strict preference C₁≻C₆ contradicts it, so transitivity is violated.

q: For a consumer with a bliss point, moving beyond the bliss point violates:
explain: Past a bliss point more of a good lowers utility, so 'more is better' — monotonicity — fails there.

q: In the lecture, “well-behaved” preferences are monotonic, convex, and:
explain: In the course, 'well-behaved' preferences are monotonic, convex and continuous.

q: Good y is a “bad” (y vertical, good x horizontal). Its indifference curves are:
explain: If y is a bad, more y lowers utility, so to stay indifferent an increase in the good x must be matched by more of the bad y — the indifference curve slopes upward.

q: Perfect substitutes have indifference curves that are:
explain: Perfect substitutes have a constant MRS, so their indifference curves are straight lines with constant slope.

q: If good 1 (horizontal axis) is a neutral good, its indifference curves are:
explain: A neutral good on the horizontal axis does not affect utility, so utility depends only on good 2; indifference curves are horizontal lines (constant good 2).

q: “More is better” is the everyday name for:
explain: 'More is better' is the everyday statement of monotonicity.

q: Which indifference curve does NOT slope downward?
explain: If good 2 (vertical axis) is a bad, its indifference curves slope upward, not downward; the other cases all slope down.
opts: one where good 2 is a bad

q: The indifference “curves” for a bliss point look like:
explain: Around a bliss point utility falls in every direction, so indifference sets are closed loops (concentric ovals) around it.
opts: closed loops around the bliss point

q: Completeness means:
explain: Completeness means any two bundles can be compared: A≽B, B≽A, or both.
opts: any two bundles can be compared

q: If indifference curves are straight, downward-sloping lines, the two goods are:
explain: Straight, downward-sloping indifference lines (constant MRS) are the signature of perfect substitutes.

q: Strictly convex preferences have indifference curves that are:
explain: Strictly convex preferences give indifference curves that bow toward the origin (diminishing MRS).

q: Transitivity is the assumption that rules out:
explain: Transitivity rules out crossing indifference curves; a crossing would violate the consistency A≽B, B≽C ⇒ A≽C.

q: A consumer likes pepperoni (horizontal) and dislikes anchovies (vertical). The curves:
explain: Pepperoni is a good (horizontal), anchovies a bad (vertical); to stay indifferent more pepperoni must be offset by more anchovies, so the curve slopes upward.

q: Weak monotonicity says:
explain: Weak monotonicity: a bundle with at least as much of every good is at least as good (a weak improvement).
opts: more of every good makes you at least as well off
you can always rank two bundles

q: Strict convexity makes the indifference curve:
explain: Strict convexity makes indifference curves bow toward the origin.

q: Which pairing gives L-shaped curves?
explain: A left and a right shoe are consumed in fixed proportion (perfect complements), giving L-shaped indifference curves.
opts: a left and a right shoe

q: A dog ignores collar colour (horizontal axis); only treats (vertical) matter. The curves are:
explain: Collar colour on the horizontal axis is a neutral good, so utility depends only on treats (vertical); indifference curves are horizontal lines.

q: Diminishing MRS means that, moving right along the curve, the consumer gives up:
explain: Diminishing MRS: moving right (more good 1), the consumer gives up less and less good 2 per additional unit of good 1.

q: Transitivity guarantees:
explain: Transitivity guarantees indifference curves do not cross.

q: Continuity guarantees:
explain: Continuity guarantees no sudden jumps in preference: bundles close together are ranked similarly.

q: Perfect substitutes u=2x+3y have a constant MRS (of x for y) equal to:
explain: MRS of x for y = MUx/MUy = 2/3 for u=2x+3y, and it is constant (perfect substitutes).

q: Which is NOT one of the three rationality axioms?
explain: The three rationality axioms are completeness, transitivity and reflexivity; convexity is a shape assumption, not a rationality axiom.

q: Which is NOT part of “well-behaved” preferences (lecture version)?
explain: 'Well-behaved' preferences are monotonic, convex and continuous; completeness is a separate rationality axiom, not part of the well-behaved shape assumptions.

q: If more of a good eventually makes you worse off (satiation), which fails there?
explain: Satiation means more of a good eventually lowers utility, which violates monotonicity ('more is better').

q: Straight, parallel, downward-sloping indifference lines belong to:
explain: Straight, parallel, downward-sloping indifference lines (constant MRS) represent perfect substitutes.

q: For u=min(x,y) at a bundle with x=y, adding only more x:
explain: For u=min(x,y) at x=y the goods are balanced; adding only more x raises the larger argument, so the min — and utility — is unchanged.

q: A consumer who likes variety has indifference curves that are:
explain: A taste for variety means averages are preferred to extremes (convexity), so indifference curves bow toward the origin.

q: Two indifference curves from the same preference map:
explain: Two indifference curves from one consistent (transitive) preference map can never cross.

q: With a good on the horizontal axis and a bad on the vertical axis, higher utility is found by moving:
explain: With a good on the horizontal axis and a bad on the vertical, utility rises by getting more of the good and less of the bad — moving down and to the right.

q: Strict monotonicity rules out indifference curves that are:
explain: Strong (strict) monotonicity forbids flat or vertical segments, since adding to either good must strictly improve the bundle.

q: The slope of an indifference curve is called the:
explain: The (absolute) slope of an indifference curve is the marginal rate of substitution (MRS).

q: A dog prefers park to yard and yard to couch. By transitivity it prefers:
explain: Transitivity applied to strict preference: park≻yard and yard≻couch imply park≻couch.

q: Which utility function represents perfect complements?
explain: u=min(x,y) is the fixed-proportion (Leontief) form representing perfect complements.

q: Reflexivity of preferences says that:
explain: Reflexivity states that every bundle is at least as good as itself (X≽X); it is one of the three rationality axioms alongside completeness and transitivity.
opts: every bundle is at least as good as itself
any two bundles can be ranked

q: Local non-satiation means that, however small the neighbourhood around a bundle, there is:
explain: Local non-satiation: for any bundle and any radius ε there exists a bundle within ε that is strictly preferred, ruling out thick indifference bands and local bliss points.
opts: a nearby bundle that is strictly preferred

q: Under monotonicity, an indifference curve lying farther from the origin represents:
explain: Monotonicity (more is better) means a bundle with more of both goods is preferred, so indifference curves farther from the origin are strictly better.
opts: a strictly higher level of utility

q: If u(x,y)=xy represents a consumer's preferences, which function represents the SAME preferences?
explain: Utility is ordinal: only strictly increasing transforms preserve preferences. ln x + ln y = ln(xy) applies the increasing function ln to xy (same ranking); the other three are decreasing in xy and reverse the order. Verified by identical MRS = y/x.

q: Applying which transformation to a utility function would CHANGE the preferences it represents?
explain: Only strictly increasing transforms preserve preferences. g(u)=−u is strictly decreasing (g′=−1 less than 0), so it reverses the ranking; +5, ×2 and ln are strictly increasing and leave preferences unchanged.
opts: taking logs, g(u)=ln u for u greater than 0

q: Perfect complements u=min(x,y) satisfy weak monotonicity but fail strong monotonicity because, starting from x=y:
explain: Strong monotonicity requires that adding to even one good makes you strictly better off. At x=y, min(x,y) is unchanged when only the abundant good rises, so strong monotonicity fails while weak monotonicity (more of BOTH is at least as good) still holds.
opts: adding only one good leaves utility unchanged

q: The marginal rate of substitution (MRS) at a bundle equals:
explain: The MRS is the (absolute) slope of the indifference curve, equal to the ratio of marginal utilities MUx/MUy — the amount of good 2 the consumer will trade for one more unit of good 1 at constant utility.
opts: the absolute slope of the indifference curve, MUx/MUy
the slope of the budget line

q: Moving down-right along a convex indifference curve (more x₁, less x₂), diminishing MRS means:
explain: Moving right, x₁ becomes abundant and x₂ scarce, so MUx falls and MUy rises; the ratio MRS = MUx/MUy declines. That is diminishing MRS, the hallmark of convex preferences.
opts: MUx falls relative to MUy, so the MRS shrinks

q: Bundles A = (5,5) and B = (6,4). Strong monotonicity ALONE tells us:
explain: Monotonicity ranks a bundle above another only when it has at least as much of every good. Here A has more x₂ but less x₁, so neither dominates and monotonicity alone cannot rank them.
opts: nothing — neither bundle has at least as much of BOTH goods
A is strictly preferred to B
B is strictly preferred to A

q: A consumer says: “I simply cannot compare bundle A and bundle B.” This directly violates:
explain: Completeness requires that for any two bundles the consumer can state A≽B, B≽A, or both; declaring two bundles incomparable violates completeness (not transitivity, which concerns chains of rankings).

q: A consumer prefers A to B and B to C, but also prefers C to A. Which axiom fails — and which still holds?
explain: Transitivity requires A≽B and B≽C ⇒ A≽C; the cycle A≻B≻C≻A contradicts it. Every pair is still ranked, so completeness is satisfied — the consumer is complete but intransitive.

q: For u = x²y, the MRS (= MUx/MUy) at (x,y) = (2,3) is:
explain: MUx = 2xy = 12 and MUy = x² = 4, so MRS = 12/4 = 3 (equivalently MRS = (a/b)(y/x) = (2/1)(3/2) = 3). The distractors 6 and 12 are the raw marginal utilities.

q: Which single axiom, by itself, forces indifference curves to be both thin (not thick) and downward-sloping?
explain: Monotonicity ('more is better') implies that a bundle with more of both goods is strictly preferred; this rules out thick indifference bands and forces the curve to slope downward. Transitivity only prevents crossings; completeness and continuity say nothing about slope.

q: Bruno the dog strictly prefers a big treat to a small treat, and a small treat to a pat. If his preferences are transitive, he must:
explain: Transitivity applied to strict preference: big≻small and small≻pat imply big≻pat.
opts: strictly prefer a big treat to a pat
prefer a pat to a big treat
be indifferent between a big treat and a pat

q: u = xy and v = x²y² rank all bundles identically. A quick check that they give the SAME indifference map is that:
explain: v = (xy)² is the increasing transform g(u)=u² of u=xy, so it represents the same preferences; both have MRS = MUx/MUy = y/x, so their indifference curves coincide.
opts: both have MRS = y/x at every bundle
v has twice the MRS of u

q: Local non-satiation is WEAKER than monotonicity because it also permits:
explain: Monotonicity says more of every good is better; local non-satiation only requires a strictly better bundle arbitrarily close by. The latter still rules out thick curves but allows a 'bad' (you improve by consuming less of it).
opts: a good to be a 'bad', as long as a strictly better bundle always exists nearby

q: The MRS at a bundle is determined by:
explain: MRS is the slope of the indifference curve — a feature of preferences. Prices set the budget line's slope; the two are equated only at an interior optimum, but the MRS itself is a preference concept.
opts: the consumer's preferences (indifference-curve slope) at that bundle

q: The transform g(u) = u² preserves the preferences represented by u only when:
explain: g(u)=u² is strictly increasing only for u ≥ 0 (g′=2u greater than 0 there); if utility can be negative, squaring is not monotonic and scrambles the ranking. For non-negative utilities (e.g. u=xy on the positive quadrant) it is a valid monotonic transform.
opts: utility is non-negative, so g is increasing on its range

q: For an ORDINAL utility function with u(A) = 10 and u(B) = 5, we may correctly conclude only that:
explain: Ordinal utility conveys only ranking: u(A) greater than u(B) means A≻B. Because any strictly increasing transform is allowed, the ratio 10/5 and the gap 10−5 carry no meaning — only the order does.
opts: A is exactly twice as good as B
the utility gap A−B is meaningful
B gives half the satisfaction of A

q: Higher indifference curves being preferred to lower ones is a direct consequence of:
explain: Monotonicity ('more is better') is what makes bundles on indifference curves farther from the origin — which contain more of the goods — preferred.

q: Price elasticity of demand measures:
explain: Own-price elasticity measures how quantity demanded responds to a price change: ε = (dq/dp)(p/q).
opts: how much quantity responds to a price change
how much price responds to quantity

q: Demand is “elastic” when the elasticity in absolute value is:
explain: Demand is elastic when the elasticity exceeds 1 in absolute value.

q: A 10% price rise cuts quantity demanded by 20%. Demand is:
explain: The size of the elasticity is 20 percent over 10 percent = 2, which exceeds 1, so demand is elastic.

q: Which good is likely the most price-inelastic?
explain: Insulin is a life-saving necessity with no substitutes, so its demand is the most price-inelastic.
opts: one brand of cola among many

q: More available substitutes make demand:
explain: More substitutes let buyers switch away more easily, so demand becomes more elastic.

q: For an inelastic good, raising the price makes total revenue:
explain: For inelastic demand quantity falls proportionally less than the price rises, so total revenue rises.

q: A negative income elasticity means the good is:
explain: A negative income elasticity defines an inferior good.

q: If the cross-price elasticity between two goods is positive, they are:
explain: A positive cross-price elasticity means the two goods are substitutes.

q: Over a longer time horizon, demand for a good usually becomes:
explain: Over a longer horizon buyers adjust more, so demand becomes more elastic.

q: John's demand is more elastic than Jim's. After a price rise, John cuts his quantity:
explain: More elastic demand means a larger quantity response, so John cuts his quantity more than Jim.

q: A perfectly inelastic demand curve is:
explain: Perfectly inelastic demand is a vertical line: quantity is fixed regardless of price.

q: A perfectly elastic demand curve is:
explain: Perfectly elastic demand is horizontal: any quantity is bought at one price.

q: Unit elastic demand has an elasticity (absolute value) of:
explain: Unit-elastic demand has an elasticity of 1 in absolute value.

q: The own-price elasticity of demand is usually:
explain: Because demand slopes down, the own-price elasticity is normally negative.

q: If total revenue rises when the price falls, demand is:
explain: If a price cut raises total revenue, demand must be elastic.

q: A luxury good has an income elasticity that is:
explain: A luxury has an income elasticity greater than 1.

q: A normal necessity has an income elasticity that is:
explain: A normal necessity has an income elasticity between 0 and 1.

q: The cross-price elasticity of two substitutes (coffee and tea) is:
explain: Substitutes have a positive cross-price elasticity.

q: The cross-price elasticity of two complements (cars and petrol) is:
explain: Complements have a negative cross-price elasticity.

q: Along a straight-line demand curve, demand is more elastic:
explain: A straight-line demand curve is more elastic near the top, where price is high and quantity low.

q: At the midpoint of a linear demand curve, demand is:
explain: The midpoint of a linear demand curve is the unit-elastic point (elasticity 1 in absolute value).

q: If a 5% price increase leaves quantity unchanged, demand is:
explain: If quantity does not respond at all to price, demand is perfectly inelastic.

q: A firm wanting to raise revenue should raise its price if demand is:
explain: On the inelastic part revenue rises with price, so a firm raises revenue by raising price when demand is inelastic.

q: Which makes demand more inelastic?
explain: A good that takes only a tiny share of the budget has more inelastic demand.
opts: the good is a tiny part of the budget

q: Salt's demand is inelastic mainly because:
explain: Salt is a tiny-budget necessity with no close substitutes, so its demand is inelastic.
opts: it is a tiny necessity with no substitutes

q: A Giffen good must be:
explain: A Giffen good is an inferior good whose income effect outweighs the substitution effect.

q: Demand tends to be more elastic when the good is defined:
explain: Narrowly defined goods have more substitutes, which makes demand more elastic.

q: If elasticity equals -0.4, a price rise makes total revenue:
explain: The size of the elasticity, 0.4, is below 1, so demand is inelastic and a price rise raises total revenue.

q: An income elasticity of +2.5 tells you the good is:
explain: An income elasticity of +2.5 exceeds 1, so the good is a normal luxury.

q: Two goods with a cross-price elasticity of zero are:
explain: A zero cross-price elasticity means the goods are unrelated (independent).

q: Demand x=0.025m−0.125p, with m=120 and p=20. Current own-price elasticity of demand? (write the sign) [ε=(∂x/∂p)(p/x), x=3−2.5=0.5]
Elis has homothetic preferences. At income 500 she bought 10 books and 15 magazines. At income 400 (same prices) she buys:
explain: Homothetic preferences scale quantities with income: at 400/500 = 0.8 of income she buys 0.8·(10,15) = (8,12).
a: 8 books and 12 magazines (homothetic ⇒ quantities scale with income, ×0.8).

q: Elasticity of demand for textbooks is −0.1; price rises 20%. Quantity change?
explain: Percentage change in quantity = ε·(percentage change in price) = minus 0.1·20 = minus 2 percent, so quantity falls 2 percent.
a: Quantity demanded decreases by 2% (−0.1 × 20%).

q: Two goods, one is Giffen. If the Giffen good's price falls (other price fixed), the demand for the OTHER good:
explain: If the Giffen good's price falls, its own quantity falls (Giffen), freeing budget; with only two goods all freed spending shifts, so the other good's demand must rise.
a: Must increase.

q: Income rises 20,000 → 25,000 (+25%); demand rises 30 → 60 (+100%). Which is correct?
explain: Percentage change in quantity is (60 minus 30)/30 = 100 percent and income change is (25000 minus 20000)/20000 = 25 percent, so income elasticity = 100/25 = 4, above 1, a luxury.
a: The good is likely a luxury (income elasticity = 100/25 = 4 > 1).

q: Pat's price elasticity of demand for bread is −0.2 at CZK 30. Mat has the same demand. Their aggregate demand's price elasticity at CZK 30 is:
explain: Horizontally summing two identical demands doubles quantity at every price but leaves the elasticity unchanged, so it stays minus 0.2.
a: −0.2 (elasticity is unchanged by horizontally adding identical demands).

q: Denis sold an inherited cottage (1,000,000) and now spends more on holidays abroad. Which is correct?
explain: Extra wealth from selling the cottage raised holiday spending, so holidays are a normal good and the income-offer curve slopes up; more than one statement is therefore correct.
a: More of these are correct — holidays are a normal good for Denis and his income-offer curve is increasing.

q: x and y are perfect substitutes (1-for-1) and y is cheaper. The income-offer curve is:
explain: With one-for-one substitutes he spends everything on the cheaper good y at every income, so the income-offer curve runs along the y-axis.
a: A line coinciding with the axis measuring good y (he spends everything on the cheaper good y).

q: Demand is downward-sloping and price-INELASTIC. Which is correct?
explain: Inelastic means the elasticity is below 1 in absolute value, so a 1 percent price fall raises quantity by less than 1 percent.
a: With a 1% price fall, quantity rises by less than 1%.

q: Alisha's demand for rice is (m−p_l)/(2p_r). Which is true?
explain: For q_rice = (m minus p_l)/(2·p_r): the derivative with respect to m is 1/(2·p_r), which is positive (normal), and with respect to p_l is minus 1/(2·p_r), which is negative (a gross complement of lentils).
a: Rice is a normal good and a gross complement of lentils (demand rises with m, falls as p_l rises).

q: The own-price elasticity of demand is defined as:
explain: Own-price elasticity is the proportional response of quantity to price, (dq/dp)(p/q).

q: A good whose own-price elasticity of demand is positive (quantity rises when its own price rises) is:
explain: A positive own-price elasticity is the defining signature of a Giffen good.

q: Demand is q = 100 minus 2p. At p=10 the own-price elasticity is:
explain: q = 80, so ε = (dq/dp)(p/q) = minus 2·(10/80) = minus 0.25 (inelastic near the bottom).

q: For q = 100 minus 2p, at p=40 the own-price elasticity is:
explain: q = 20, so ε = minus 2·(40/20) = minus 4 (elastic near the top).

q: For q = 50 minus p, at p=30 the own-price elasticity is:
explain: q = 20, so ε = minus 1·(30/20) = minus 1.5, which is elastic.

q: For q = 200 minus 4p, at p=25 the own-price elasticity is:
explain: q = 100, so ε = minus 4·(25/100) = minus 1, the unit-elastic point.

q: For q = 300 minus 5p, at p=20 the own-price elasticity is:
explain: q = 200, so ε = minus 5·(20/200) = minus 0.5 (inelastic).

q: For the demand q = 100/p, the own-price elasticity is:
explain: A constant-elasticity demand q = 100·p^(minus 1) has elasticity minus 1 at every price.

q: For q = 40 minus 2p, at p=15 the own-price elasticity is:
explain: q = 10, so ε = minus 2·(15/10) = minus 3 (elastic).

q: For q = 500 minus 10p, at p=25 the own-price elasticity is:
explain: q = 250, so ε = minus 10·(25/250) = minus 1, the unit-elastic midpoint.

q: Between the points (p=10, q=100) and (p=12, q=80), the arc (midpoint) elasticity is:
explain: Arc ε uses midpoints: (minus 20/90)/(2/11) = minus 11/9.

q: Income rises from 100 to 150 and quantity from 20 to 40. The income elasticity is:
explain: Percentage change in quantity 100 percent over income change 50 percent gives 2, above 1, a luxury.

q: Income rises from 200 to 240 and quantity from 50 to 55. The income elasticity is:
explain: Quantity change 10 percent over income change 20 percent gives 0.5, between 0 and 1, a necessity.

q: When the price of tea rises 10 percent, the quantity of coffee bought rises 5 percent. The cross-price elasticity is:
explain: Cross elasticity = +5/+10 = +0.5; a positive sign means substitutes.

q: When the price of petrol rises 20 percent, the quantity of cars bought falls 4 percent. The cross-price elasticity is:
explain: Cross elasticity = minus 4/+20 = minus 0.2; a negative sign means complements.

q: If demand is price-inelastic, a rise in price makes total revenue:
explain: When |ε| is below 1 quantity falls proportionally less than price rises, so revenue rises.

q: Total revenue is maximised at the point of the demand curve where demand is:
explain: Revenue peaks where marginal revenue is zero, which is the unit-elastic point (|ε| = 1).

q: If demand is price-elastic, a rise in price makes total revenue:
explain: When |ε| exceeds 1 quantity falls proportionally more than price rises, so revenue falls.

q: For the constant-elasticity demand q = 50·p⁻³, the own-price elasticity is:
explain: For q = k·p^(minus n) the elasticity is minus n everywhere, here minus 3.

q: Demand for film tickets is q = 60 minus 3p. At p=10 the own-price elasticity is:
explain: q = 30, so ε = minus 3·(10/30) = minus 1, exactly unit elastic.

q: Two identical consumers each have own-price elasticity minus 0.8 at p=30. The market (horizontally summed) demand at p=30 has elasticity:
explain: Horizontally adding identical demands scales quantity but leaves the elasticity unchanged at minus 0.8.

q: For the linear demand q = 500 minus 10p, demand is unit elastic at the price:
explain: Solving minus 10p/(500 minus 10p) = minus 1 gives p = 25 (the midpoint).

q: Between the points (p=20, q=100) and (p=25, q=75), the arc (midpoint) elasticity is:
For the linear demand q = 100 minus 2p, demand is unit elastic at the price:
explain: Solving minus 2p/(100 minus 2p) = minus 1 gives 4p = 100, so p = 25 (the midpoint).

q: For q = 120 minus 3p, demand is elastic (|ε| greater than 1) for prices above:
explain: The unit-elastic price solves minus 3p/(120 minus 3p) = minus 1, giving p = 20; above it demand is elastic.

q: For the constant-elasticity demand q = 100·p⁻², the own-price elasticity is:
explain: For q = k·p^(minus 2) the elasticity is minus 2 at every price.

q: Between (p=4, q=120) and (p=6, q=80), the arc (midpoint) elasticity is:
explain: Arc ε = (minus 40/100)/(2/5) = minus 1, unit elastic over this range.

q: For q = 100 minus 2p, demand is more elastic at:
explain: At p=40, ε = minus 4; at p=10, ε = minus 0.25; the larger size at p=40 means it is more elastic there.

q: Income rises 25 percent and quantity falls 5 percent. The income elasticity is:
explain: Income elasticity = minus 5/+25 = minus 0.2; the negative sign marks an inferior good.

q: Demand is x = 0.04m minus 0.5p, giving x = 30 at m=1000, p=20. The income elasticity of demand is:
explain: Income elasticity = (dx/dm)(m/x) = 0.04·(1000/30) = 4/3, so at this point x is a luxury.

q: Demand for good x is qx = 40 minus 2·px + 3·py. At px=5, py=4, the cross-price elasticity with respect to py is:
explain: qx = 42 and dqx/dpy = 3, so cross ε = 3·(4/42) = 2/7, positive, so substitutes.

q: The price of good B rises from 5 to 6 and the quantity of good A rises from 100 to 110. The arc cross-price elasticity is:
explain: Arc cross ε = (10/105)/(1/5.5) = 11/21, positive, so A and B are substitutes.

q: For q = 100 minus 2p, total revenue p·q is maximised at the price:
explain: TR = p(100 minus 2p); setting dTR/dp = 100 minus 4p = 0 gives p = 25 (the unit-elastic point).

q: For q = 100 minus 2p, raising the price from 10 to 11 changes total revenue by:
explain: TR goes from 10·80 = 800 to 11·78 = 858, a rise of 58, because demand is inelastic there.

q: A linear demand q = a minus b·p has elasticity minus 1.5 at the point p=30, q=40. The slope coefficient b is:
explain: From minus b·(30/40) = minus 1.5 we get b = 1.5·40/30 = 2.

q: For q = 40 minus 2p, demand is unit elastic at the price:
explain: Solving minus 2p/(40 minus 2p) = minus 1 gives 4p = 40, so p = 10 (the midpoint).

q: For q = 80 minus 4p, the own-price elasticity equals minus 3 at the price:
explain: Solving minus 4p/(80 minus 4p) = minus 3 gives 16p = 240, so p = 15.

q: For q = 90 minus 3p at p=20, the own-price elasticity is:
explain: q = 30, so ε = minus 3·(20/30) = minus 2, elastic, so a price rise would lower total revenue.

q: A consumer with u = min(3x, 4y) faces px=2, py=1. The own-price elasticity of demand for good y is:
explain: For these complements y = m/((4/3)px + py) and its own-price elasticity is minus 3py/(4px+3py) = minus 3/11.

q: For the constant-elasticity demand q = 100·p^(minus 0.5), the own-price elasticity everywhere is:
explain: For q = k·p^(minus n) the elasticity is minus n, here minus 0.5, inelastic at every price.

q: Two goods are gross substitutes if ∂ x<sub>1</sub>/∂ p<sub>2</sub> is:
explain: By definition gross substitutes satisfy ∂x₁/∂p₂ greater than 0: a rise in p₂ raises demand for x₁. So the sign is positive.

q: Butter and margarine are substitutes. If butter gets cheaper, margarine demand:
explain: Substitutes: a fall in butter's price makes buyers switch toward butter, so margarine (its substitute) demand falls. The cross-price effect is positive, so p down for one lowers the other's quantity.

q: Cars and petrol are complements. If petrol gets cheaper, car demand:
explain: Complements: cheaper petrol raises the quantity of cars demanded (they are used together). Cross-price effect is negative: p_petrol down → cars up.

q: Gross complements have a cross-price effect ∂ x<sub>1</sub>/∂ p<sub>2</sub> that is:
explain: Gross complements are defined by ∂x₁/∂p₂ less than 0 (negative): a rise in p₂ lowers x₁.

q: x1 is a gross substitute of x2. If p<sub>2</sub> rises, x1 demand:
explain: Gross substitute: ∂x₁/∂p₂ greater than 0, so a rise in p₂ raises x₁ — demand rises.

q: “Gross” effects (unlike “net” effects) include:
explain: Gross (uncompensated) effects include BOTH the substitution and the income effect; net (Hicksian/compensated) effects strip the income effect out.

q: If the cross-price elasticity is negative, the goods are:
explain: A negative cross-price elasticity means p_j up → x_i down, which is the defining sign of complements.

q: A left shoe and a right shoe are:
explain: A left shoe and a right shoe are consumed together in fixed proportion — the classic perfect complements.

q: A rise in the price of tea increases the demand for coffee. Tea and coffee are:
explain: A rise in the tea price increasing coffee demand is a positive cross effect — the defining sign of substitutes.

q: x1 is a gross substitute of x2. If p<sub>2</sub> falls, x1 demand:
explain: Gross substitute: ∂x₁/∂p₂ greater than 0, so x₁ moves with p₂. p₂ falls → x₁ falls.

q: Two unrelated (independent) goods have a cross-price effect ∂ x<sub>1</sub>/∂ p<sub>2</sub> that is:
explain: Independent (unrelated) goods have zero cross-price effect: ∂x₁/∂p₂ = 0.

q: Coffee and sugar tend to be:
explain: Coffee and sugar are normally consumed together, so they are complements (negative cross effect).

q: Pepsi and Coca-Cola are:
explain: Pepsi and Coca-Cola are close substitutes, so the cross-price effect is positive.

q: If the price of good 2 rises and demand for good 1 falls, the goods are:
explain: p₂ up together with x₁ down means ∂x₁/∂p₂ less than 0 — complements.

q: Tennis rackets and tennis balls are:
explain: Rackets and balls are used together — complements.

q: The price of tea rises, so demand for coffee (a substitute):
explain: Substitutes: a rise in the tea price shifts demand toward coffee, so coffee demand rises (positive cross effect).

q: Printers and ink cartridges are:
explain: Printers and ink cartridges are used together — complements.

q: A positive cross-price elasticity means the goods are:
explain: A positive cross-price elasticity (ε_ij greater than 0) defines substitutes.

q: The price of good 2 falls and demand for good 1 rises. The goods are:
explain: p₂ down with x₁ up means ∂x₁/∂p₂ less than 0 — complements (they move in opposite directions with p₂).

q: If x1 is a gross complement of x2 and p<sub>2</sub> rises, x1 demand:
explain: Gross complement: ∂x₁/∂p₂ less than 0, so p₂ up → x₁ down (falls).

q: iPhones and Android phones are:
explain: iPhones and Android phones are substitutes — you buy one instead of the other.

q: Bread and butter are usually:
explain: Bread and butter are eaten together — complements.

q: The price of coffee rises and tea sales go up. Coffee and tea are:
explain: A rise in the coffee price raising tea sales is a positive cross effect — substitutes.

q: Hot dogs and hot dog buns are:
explain: Hot dogs and buns are consumed together — complements.

q: If ∂ x<sub>1</sub>/∂ p<sub>2</sub> = 0, the goods are:
explain: ∂x₁/∂p₂ = 0 means no cross effect, so the goods are independent/unrelated.

q: Cheaper airline tickets raise hotel bookings. Flights and hotels are:
explain: Cheaper flights raising hotel bookings is a negative cross effect (p_flight down → hotels up): complements.

q: Train tickets and plane tickets on the same route are:
explain: Train and plane on the same route are substitutes for making the trip.

q: If two goods are substitutes, a fall in the price of one:
explain: Substitutes: a fall in one good's price raises its own demand and pulls demand away from the other, so the other's demand falls.

q: If two goods are complements, a rise in the price of one:
explain: Complements: a rise in one good's price lowers demand for the other (they are used together).

q: Butter's price doubles and margarine flies off the shelves. They are:
explain: Dearer butter with margarine selling more is a positive cross effect — substitutes.

q: A cross-price elasticity of +0.8 means the goods are:
explain: ε_ij = +0.8 is greater than 0 → substitutes.

q: A cross-price elasticity of -0.8 means the goods are:
explain: ε_ij = −0.8 is less than 0 → complements.

q: A cross-price elasticity of 0 means the goods are:
explain: ε_ij = 0 means no cross effect → unrelated/independent.

q: Peanut butter and jelly are:
explain: Peanut butter and jelly are eaten together — complements.

q: Tea and coffee are:
explain: Tea and coffee are substitutes (positive cross effect).

q: If the price of x2 rises and x1 demand rises, x1 and x2 are:
explain: p₂ up with x₁ up (same direction) → ∂x₁/∂p₂ greater than 0 → substitutes.

q: If the price of x2 rises and x1 demand falls, x1 and x2 are:
explain: p₂ up with x₁ down (opposite directions) → ∂x₁/∂p₂ less than 0 → complements.

q: A game console and its games are:
explain: A console and its games are used together — complements.

q: Two goods with no cross effect are called:
explain: A zero cross effect defines independent goods.

q: Uber and traditional taxis are:
explain: Uber and traditional taxis are substitutes for a ride.

q: For Cobb-Douglas u=x<sup>a</sup> y<sup>b</sup>, demand for x does not depend on p<sub>y</sub>, so x and y are (gross):
explain: Cobb-Douglas Marshallian demand x = [a/(a+b)]·m/px contains no p_y, so ∂x/∂p_y = 0: gross-unrelated (zero cross effect).

q: Gross substitutability is:
explain: Gross (uncompensated) cross effects need not be symmetric: ∂x₁/∂p₂ can differ from ∂x₂/∂p₁ because the two income effects differ.

q: Net (compensated) cross-substitution effects ∂ h<sub>i</sub>/∂ p<sub>j</sub> are:
explain: The Slutsky substitution matrix is symmetric: ∂h_i/∂p_j = ∂h_j/∂p_i, so net (compensated) cross effects are symmetric.

q: A good can be a gross complement yet a net substitute because of:
explain: Slutsky: ∂x_i/∂p_j = ∂h_i/∂p_j − x_j·∂x_i/∂m. A positive net term (net substitute) can be flipped negative (gross complement) by a large income effect.

q: If x<sub>1</sub> = 100 - 2p<sub>1</sub> + 3p<sub>2</sub>, then ∂ x<sub>1</sub>/∂ p<sub>2</sub> = +3, so x<sub>1</sub> and x<sub>2</sub> are gross:
explain: ∂x₁/∂p₂ = +3 is greater than 0, so x₁ and x₂ are gross substitutes.

q: Perfect complements (Leontief) are, in the gross sense:
explain: Perfect complements (Leontief) demand x = m/(p₁+p₂) has ∂x/∂p₂ less than 0, so they are gross complements.

q: The cross-price elasticity of x<sub>1</sub> with respect to p<sub>2</sub> is:
explain: Cross-price elasticity = (∂x₁/∂p₂)·(p₂/x₁): the percent change in x₁ per percent change in p₂.

q: Two goods are net substitutes. By Slutsky symmetry, good 2 is:
explain: Slutsky symmetry: if good 1 is a net substitute for good 2, then good 2 is a net substitute for good 1 (∂h₁/∂p₂ = ∂h₂/∂p₁, same sign).

q: If x1 is a gross substitute of x2, is x2 necessarily a gross substitute of x1?
explain: Gross relations are not necessarily symmetric, so x₁ being a gross substitute of x₂ does not force x₂ to be a gross substitute of x₁.

q: A cross-price elasticity of -1.5 means the goods are:
explain: ε_ij = −1.5: the negative sign means complements, and magnitude greater than 1 means strong (cross-elastic).

q: Demand is x₁ = 100 − 2p₁ + 4p₂. At p₁ = 10, p₂ = 5 (so x₁ = 100), the cross-price elasticity of x₁ with respect to p₂ equals:
explain: ∂x₁/∂p₂ = 4 and x₁ = 100 − 20 + 20 = 100, so ε₁₂ = (∂x₁/∂p₂)·(p₂/x₁) = 4·(5/100) = 0.2. Positive → gross substitutes.

q: For perfect substitutes u = 2x + 3y with prices (px, py) = (1, 2) and income 12, the optimal bundle (x, y) is:
explain: Compare marginal utility per dollar: MUx/px = 2/1 = 2 versus MUy/py = 3/2 = 1.5. Since x gives more utility per dollar, spend all income on x: x = 12/1 = 12, y = 0 — a corner solution.

q: For perfect complements u = min(x, 2y) with prices (px, py) = (2, 1) and income 20, the optimal bundle (x, y) is:
explain: The optimum lies on x = 2y (nothing is wasted). Budget 2x + y = 20 with x = 2y gives 2·(2y) + y = 5y = 20, so y = 4 and x = 8.

q: For perfect complements u = min(x, y), Marshallian demand is x* = m/(px + py). The sign of ∂x*/∂py is:
explain: ∂x*/∂py = −m/(px + py)² is less than 0: a rise in py lowers x, so the goods are gross complements — as expected for Leontief preferences.

q: A 10% rise in the price of cinema tickets raises streaming subscriptions by 6%. The cross-price elasticity of streaming with respect to the cinema price is:
explain: ε = (percent change in streaming)/(percent change in cinema price) = +6/+10 = +0.6. A positive cross-price elasticity means substitutes: viewers substitute streaming for cinema.

q: Slutsky in cross form: ∂xᵢ/∂pⱼ = ∂hᵢ/∂pⱼ − xⱼ·(∂xᵢ/∂m). If ∂hᵢ/∂pⱼ = 5 (net substitutes), xⱼ = 4 and ∂xᵢ/∂m = 2, then the gross cross effect ∂xᵢ/∂pⱼ is:
explain: ∂xᵢ/∂pⱼ = 5 − 4·2 = −3, which is less than 0. The good is a NET substitute but a GROSS complement: a strong (normal-good) income effect flips the sign.

q: The Slutsky substitution matrix is symmetric. If the compensated cross effect ∂h₁/∂p₂ = 7, then ∂h₂/∂p₁ equals:
explain: Slutsky symmetry: ∂h_i/∂p_j = ∂h_j/∂p_i, so ∂h₂/∂p₁ = ∂h₁/∂p₂ = 7. Net (compensated) cross effects are always symmetric, even though gross ones need not be.

q: Demand is x₁ = 50 − 3p₁ − 2p₂. At p₁ = 5, p₂ = 10 (so x₁ = 15), the cross-price elasticity ε₁₂ is:
explain: ∂x₁/∂p₂ = −2 and x₁ = 50 − 15 − 20 = 15, so ε₁₂ = −2·(10/15) = −20/15 = −4/3. The negative sign means complements, and magnitude greater than 1 means cross-elastic.

q: Suppose ∂x₁/∂p₂ is greater than 0 while ∂x₂/∂p₁ is less than 0. This is possible, and it shows that gross substitutability/complementarity is:
explain: Uncompensated (gross) cross effects carry different income effects for the two goods, so ∂x₁/∂p₂ and ∂x₂/∂p₁ need not be equal or even share a sign. Only the compensated (net) effects are symmetric.
opts: not necessarily symmetric — it can even differ in sign

q: For perfect substitutes u = x + y (so MRS = 1), if px = py the consumer's optimal choice is:
explain: When the price ratio equals the constant MRS = 1, every point on the budget line yields the same utility, so demand is indeterminate. Off this knife-edge the consumer goes to a corner (all of the cheaper good).
opts: any bundle on the budget line — demand is indeterminate
only the corner with all x
only the corner with all y

q: p<sub>x</sub> decreases, holding the consumer's utility fixed at its original level. The substitution effect on the quantity demanded of x is:
explain: px falls with utility held fixed, so x is relatively cheaper and compensated (Hicksian) demand for x rises; the own substitution effect always moves opposite to the price change.
opts: positive, the quantity of x rises
negative, the quantity of x falls
impossible to sign without knowing the income elasticity

q: p<sub>x</sub> increases. The own substitution effect on the demand for x is:
explain: A price rise makes x relatively dearer, so compensated demand for x falls: the own substitution effect is negative, never ambiguous.
opts: ambiguous, it depends on whether x is normal or inferior

q: The substitution effect is defined by adjusting income just enough to hold constant:
explain: The substitution effect isolates the pure relative-price change by holding real purchasing power (utility) fixed, not nominal income.
opts: the consumer's utility level (real purchasing power)
the quantity of the other good, y

q: Why can the own substitution effect never run in the same direction as the price change?
explain: Compensated demand minimizes expenditure for fixed utility; when a good becomes relatively cheaper it is weakly more attractive, so the own SE cannot move with the price.
opts: because all consumers are risk averse
because nominal income never changes in reality
because the total effect always dominates the substitution effect
because compensated demand minimizes expenditure for a fixed utility level, so the relatively cheaper good must become weakly more attractive

q: For a well-behaved consumer, the sign of the compensated (Hicksian) own-price derivative ∂ x<sup>h</sup>/∂ p<sub>x</sub> is:
explain: For well-behaved convex preferences the compensated own-price derivative ∂hx/∂px ≤ 0, equal to zero only at a Leontief kink.
opts: non-positive, strictly negative or zero only at a kink

q: The substitution effect is best described as the change in:
explain: The substitution effect is the movement along one indifference curve: the change in Hicksian (compensated) demand holding utility fixed.

q: Which classification of the good, normal, inferior, or Giffen, can flip the SIGN of the OWN substitution effect?
explain: The own substitution effect is non-positive regardless of normal, inferior, or Giffen; classification affects only the income effect.
opts: none of them; the own SE sign never depends on this classification

q: Bruno has two treat brands, A and B, that make him equally happy. The shop drops the price of A but takes back just enough allowance to keep Bruno exactly as happy as before. Due to the substitution effect alone, Bruno's consumption of A:
explain: Compensated to the same happiness, brand A is relatively cheaper, so the pure substitution effect raises A.
opts: rises, because A is now relatively cheaper
rises or falls depending on Bruno's income

q: A triathlete holds her fitness (utility) fixed while the rental cost of a bike falls. The substitution effect alone predicts she reallocates training time toward cycling because:
explain: Holding fitness (utility) fixed, cheaper cycling is the better bargain, so the substitution effect shifts time toward cycling.
opts: cycling became relatively cheaper, and holding fitness fixed she chases the best bargain
the price of running fell too

q: If, hypothetically, the own substitution effect for a price fall in x were negative, this would violate:
explain: A negative own SE for a price fall would violate the compensated law of demand (expenditure minimization under convex preferences).
opts: the basic logic of expenditure minimization under convex preferences, the compensated law of demand
the definition of a normal good
nothing; it is a common outcome for Giffen goods

q: For perfect complements (Leontief, L-shaped indifference curves), the own substitution effect for either good is:
explain: Leontief curves give no scope to substitute; the compensated bundle stays at the fixed ratio, so the own SE is zero.
opts: zero, since the compensated bundle cannot substitute away from the fixed kink ratio

q: Hicksian (Hicks) compensation adjusts income to keep constant:
explain: Hicks compensation holds utility fixed: the consumer stays on the original indifference curve.
opts: the original bundle's affordability at new prices
the utility level, the consumer stays on the original indifference curve

q: Slutsky compensation adjusts income to keep constant:
explain: Slutsky compensation holds constant the ability to just afford the ORIGINAL bundle at the new prices.
opts: the ability to just afford the ORIGINAL bundle at the new prices

q: For a price FALL, which compensation scheme leaves the consumer with LESS income, i.e. is more austere?
explain: For a price fall, reaching exactly the old utility costs no more than keeping the old bundle affordable, so Hicks removes more income and leaves less.
opts: Slutsky, since it only imposes affordability of the old bundle
they always remove exactly the same amount of income
neither; both schemes add income when price falls
Hicks, because holding utility fixed exactly at the old indifference curve is stingier than merely keeping the old bundle affordable

q: In a diagram with indifference curve IC<sub>0</sub> and old bundle A, the Hicks compensated line is tangent to IC<sub>0</sub>, while the Slutsky compensated line:
explain: The Slutsky line uses the new price ratio (parallel to the Hicks line) but is pinned through the old bundle A, so it need not be tangent to IC0.
opts: is also tangent to IC<sub>0</sub>, at the same point as Hicks
is parallel to the Hicks line (same new price ratio) but passes exactly through the old bundle A, so it need not be tangent to IC<sub>0</sub>
has a different slope than the Hicks line

q: As the size of the price change shrinks toward zero, the Slutsky and Hicks substitution effects:
explain: For an infinitesimal price change the Slutsky and Hicks substitution effects coincide (they agree to first order).
opts: always stay in a fixed ratio of two to one
converge to the same value; they agree in the first-order (infinitesimal) limit

q: Which statement correctly contrasts the two compensation schemes?
explain: Slutsky compensation uses only observed quantities and prices; Hicks compensation requires the unobservable utility/indifference map.
opts: Slutsky compensation is directly observable from market data (old quantities and both price vectors), while Hicks compensation requires knowing the unobservable utility function
only Hicks compensation is used in applied work; Slutsky gives the wrong sign
Hicks compensation requires nominal income to rise whenever price falls
Slutsky compensation always coincides exactly with the uncompensated (total) effect

q: For a price DECREASE, the Slutsky-compensated bundle reaches, compared to the original indifference curve IC<sub>0</sub>:
explain: Under a price fall the old bundle is affordable at Slutsky income, and re-optimizing can only do better, so the Slutsky bundle sits on a weakly higher indifference curve than IC0.
opts: a strictly lower indifference curve, always
exactly the same indifference curve, always
an indifference curve that cannot be ranked in general
a weakly higher indifference curve, because the old bundle is feasible for Hicks's cost-minimization, so Hicks can do at least as well for less

q: Despite differing in magnitude, the Slutsky and Hicks own-price substitution effects always agree on:
explain: Slutsky and Hicks own-price substitution effects can differ in magnitude but always share the same non-positive sign.
opts: the exact numerical magnitude, for any price change however large
the sign: both are non-positive, i.e. opposite to the price change
the size of the income effect

q: In the two-good diagram, both the Hicks and the Slutsky compensated budget lines are drawn using:
explain: Both compensated budget lines carry the NEW price ratio (parallel to budget1); they differ only in intercept (income).
opts: the OLD price ratio, parallel to budget0
the NEW price ratio: both lines are parallel to budget1; only their intercepts (incomes) differ

q: An exam trap: p<sub>x</sub> falls and the question asks for the sign of the Hicksian substitution effect on x. A student who instead (incorrectly) computes it via Slutsky compensation gets:
explain: For a price fall both methods give a positive own substitution effect; using Slutsky instead of Hicks changes only the magnitude, not the sign.
opts: the same sign, positive, just a slightly different exact magnitude
zero regardless of which method is used

q: The compensation concept that keeps the consumer on exactly the SAME indifference curve is named after:
explain: Holding the consumer on the same indifference curve is Hicks (Hicksian) compensation.

q: For a NORMAL good, following a price fall, the income effect:
explain: For a normal good a price fall raises real income and demand, reinforcing the substitution effect (both raise x).
opts: opposes the substitution effect and dominates it
reinforces (points in the same direction as) the substitution effect
opposes the substitution effect but is smaller

q: For an INFERIOR but non-Giffen good, following a price fall, the total (Marshallian) effect on quantity demanded is:
explain: An inferior non-Giffen good has an income effect that opposes but is smaller than the substitution effect, so a price fall still raises quantity.
opts: negative, because the income effect wins
impossible to determine even in principle
positive: the substitution effect still dominates the smaller, opposing income effect

q: A Giffen good is best defined as a good for which:
explain: A Giffen good is inferior with an income effect so strong it outweighs the always-negative substitution effect, so demand rises with price.
opts: it is inferior with an income effect so strong that it outweighs the substitution effect, making the total demand curve slope upward
the substitution effect is positive for a price rise
demand is completely unresponsive to price
it is a luxury with income elasticity above one

q: For a Giffen good, when its price falls, the OWN substitution effect is:
explain: Even for a Giffen good the own substitution effect is normal (positive for a price fall); only the income effect is anomalous.
opts: negative; that is precisely what makes it Giffen
positive, exactly like for every other good; it is the income effect, not the SE, that is unusual
undefined, because Giffen goods have no indifference curves

q: Which statement is TRUE about the substitution effect across normal, inferior, and Giffen goods, for a price fall?
explain: The substitution effect is positive for a price fall for every good; only the sign and size of the income effect distinguish the classes.
opts: the SE is positive for normal, negative for inferior, negative for Giffen goods
the SE is always positive, regardless of the normal, inferior, or Giffen classification; only the income effect's sign and size vary
the SE is undefined for inferior and Giffen goods
the SE equals the total effect for inferior goods

q: Every Giffen good must also be:
explain: A Giffen good must be inferior; a strong negative income effect is what overturns the law of demand.

q: Every Giffen good is inferior, but the converse fails because:
explain: Every Giffen good is inferior, but inferiority alone is not enough: Giffen also needs the income effect to outweigh the substitution effect.
opts: not every inferior good is Giffen; Giffen additionally requires the income effect to be strong enough to overturn the substitution effect
every inferior good is automatically Giffen too
inferior goods do not exist in practice
Giffen goods are actually normal goods, just measured incorrectly

q: The own substitution effect is unambiguous in sign. Which effect CAN be ambiguous, depending on the good's classification?
explain: The own substitution effect is unambiguously signed; the total (Marshallian) effect can be ambiguous because it also contains the income effect.
opts: the total (Marshallian, uncompensated) effect, because it also embeds the income effect

q: A CROSS substitution effect (the compensated effect of p<sub>y</sub> on the demand for x) differs from the OWN substitution effect in that:
explain: Unlike the own SE (always non-positive), the cross substitution effect can be positive (net substitutes) or negative (net complements).
opts: it can be positive (net substitutes) or negative (net complements), unlike the own effect, which is always non-positive with respect to its own price
it is always exactly equal to the own effect
it never appears in the Slutsky equation

q: A key symmetry result for compensated (Hicksian) cross-price effects states that:
explain: Slutsky symmetry: the compensated cross-effect of py on x equals that of px on y (∂hx/∂py = ∂hy/∂px).
opts: the cross effect always equals the own effect
cross effects are symmetric only for Cobb-Douglas utility
there is no such symmetry result in general
the cross effect of p<sub>y</sub> on x equals the cross effect of p<sub>x</sub> on y (Slutsky symmetry)

q: Mock-exam statement: p<sub>x</sub> decreases, the change in demand for x due to its own substitution effect is ____ . Given everything above, the one answer that holds NO MATTER whether x is normal, inferior, or Giffen is:
explain: For a price fall the own substitution effect is positive no matter the good's classification.
opts: ambiguous; you must know the income elasticity first

q: Price of apricots rises and you buy fewer raspberries. Consistent with:
explain: Buying fewer raspberries when apricots dearen fits the stated income and cross-price patterns (for instance both goods normal, or raspberries normal and apricots inferior).
a: Both (b) and (d): raspberries normal & apricots inferior, OR both normal.

q: Harry: u=x1·x2, last week bought (3, 25). New prices p1=6, p2=2. Minimum cost this week to be as well off as last week? [reach u0=75 cheapest: Hicksian]
explain: Old bundle gives u0 = 3·25 = 75; the cheapest cost to reach u0 at the new prices is e = 2√(p1·p2·u0) = 2√(6·2·75) = 60.

q: Price of good x changes. Which is TRUE?
explain: The own SE always opposes the price change; if the income effect runs opposite to the SE, the income effect moves with the price, which defines an inferior good.
a: If the income effect and own substitution effect work in OPPOSITE directions, x is necessarily inferior.

q: Expenditure-minimising consumer reaches u1 at (x1*,y1*) and u0 at (x0*,y0*) with u1 > u0, same prices. Then:
explain: Hicksian demand falls as utility rises exactly for an inferior good, so x1* is below x0* if and only if x is inferior.
a: x1* < x0* if and only if good x is inferior.

q: Henry: u=x+y (perfect substitutes), px=20, py=30, m=300. py drops to 15. Change in demand for y due to the SUBSTITUTION effect? [was all x; now all y]
explain: Initially px is below py so income buys only x: x=15, y=0, u0=15. Holding u0 fixed, the now-cheaper y is bought instead, giving compensated y=15, so the substitution effect on y is +15.

q: Price of oranges rises, price of chocolate constant. The change in demand from the INCOME effect alone is:
explain: A price rise for oranges lowers real income; the income effect raises orange demand only if oranges are inferior.
a: Positive if and only if orange is an inferior good.

q: Monotonic, strictly convex prefs; x0* on Hicksian H_x(u0). Both prices rise 50%; new Hicksian bundle at u0:
explain: Hicksian demand is homogeneous of degree zero in prices, so scaling all prices with utility fixed leaves the compensated bundle unchanged.
a: None of these — a proportional price rise with fixed utility leaves the Hicksian bundle unchanged.

q: Joe: u=x<sup>0.5</sup>+3y, px=1, py=6, m=10. px rises to 2. Change in demand for x from the INCOME effect? (quasilinear in y ⇒ no income effect on x)
explain: Utility is quasilinear in y, so Marshallian x depends only on prices, not income; hence the income effect on x is exactly 0.

q: Rachel: u=min(2x,2y), px=50, py=30, m=400. py rises to 50. Change in demand for muffins (y) due to the INCOME effect? (write the sign)
explain: Perfect complements have zero substitution effect, so the whole change is the income effect: y falls from 400/80=5 to 400/100=4, an income effect of −1.

q: A consumer buys 8 units of x when px = 5. px rises to 8. Under Slutsky compensation the extra income needed so the OLD bundle is still just affordable is Δm = x·Δpx. This equals:
explain: Slutsky compensation keeps the old bundle affordable: Δm = x·Δpx = 8·(8−5) = 24.

q: A consumer buying 20 units of x sees px FALL from 12 to 9. Slutsky compensation (Δm = x·Δpx) adjusts income by:
explain: Δm = x·Δpx = 20·(9−12) = −60: because the old bundle is now cheaper, Slutsky removes 60 of income.

q: Bruno's owner bought 6 bags of treats at 4 CZK each. The price rises to 7 CZK. The Slutsky compensating money that keeps the old 6-bag bundle just affordable is:
The total effect of a price rise on x is −12 and the income effect is −3. By the Slutsky decomposition the substitution effect equals:
explain: Total = SE + IE, so SE = total − IE = −12 − (−3) = −9.

q: After a price rise the substitution effect on x is −6 and the income effect is −2. The total (Marshallian) effect is:
explain: Total = SE + IE = −6 + (−2) = −8; for a normal good the income effect reinforces the substitution effect.

q: A good is inferior (but not Giffen). After its price rises the substitution effect is −6 and the income effect is +2. The total effect is:
explain: Total = SE + IE = −6 + 2 = −4: the opposing income effect shrinks but does not reverse the fall.

q: For a Giffen good after a price rise, the substitution effect is −3 and the total (Marshallian) effect is +2. The income effect must be:
explain: IE = total − SE = 2 − (−3) = +5: a large positive income effect overturns the negative substitution effect.

q: u = √(x·y), income m = 120, py = 3, and px rises from 3 to 12. Marshallian demand is x = m/(2·px). The TOTAL effect on x is:
explain: x = m/(2px): x goes from 120/6 = 20 to 120/24 = 5, a total effect of −15.

q: Same setup (u = √(x·y), m = 120, py = 3, px 3→12). Using SLUTSKY compensation (keep the old bundle affordable), the substitution effect on x is:
Same setup (u = √(x·y), m = 120, py = 3, px 3→12). Using HICKS compensation (hold the old utility), the substitution effect on x is:
explain: For this symmetric Cobb-Douglas h_x = u·√(py/px); holding u0 fixed, compensated x falls from 20 to 10, so SE = −10.

q: Same setup (u = √(x·y), m = 120, py = 3, px 3→12), where total effect = −15 and the SLUTSKY substitution effect = −7.5. The Slutsky income effect on x is:
explain: Income effect = total − substitution = −15 − (−7.5) = −7.5.

q: Same setup (u = √(x·y), m = 120, py = 3, px 3→12), where total effect = −15 and the HICKS substitution effect = −10. The Hicks income effect on x is:
explain: Income effect = total − substitution = −15 − (−10) = −5.

q: u = x + y (perfect substitutes), px = 10, py = 8, m = 80. py rises to 12. Initially only y is bought (y = 10). The Hicks substitution effect on y is:
explain: At the old prices only y is bought (y = m/py = 10, u0 = 10). At the new prices x is cheaper, so reaching u0 uses only x and compensated y = 0: SE on y = 0 − 10 = −10.

q: Same perfect-substitutes case (u = x + y, px = 10, py = 8→12, m = 80). The TOTAL (Marshallian) effect on x is:
explain: After py rises above px the consumer buys only x: x goes from 0 to m/px = 8, a total effect of +8.
