q: u = min(x, y) (perfect complements), px = 2, py = 2, m = 40. py rises to 3. The substitution effect on y is:
explain: Leontief preferences allow no substitution: the compensated bundle stays on x = y, so the substitution effect is exactly 0.

q: Same perfect-complements case (u = min(x, y), px = 2, py = 2→3, m = 40). Since the substitution effect is zero, the income effect on y equals the total effect, which is:
explain: x = y = m/(px+py): y falls from 40/4 = 10 to 40/5 = 8, so the income effect (= total) is −2.

q: u = 8·√x + y (quasilinear in y), and px rises from 1 to 4. Demand is x = 16/px². The substitution effect on x (which equals the total effect here) is:
explain: With quasilinear preferences x depends only on px, so the income effect is zero and SE = total: x falls from 16 to 1, i.e. −15.

q: Same quasilinear case (u = 8·√x + y, px 1→4, x = 16/px²). The income effect on x is:
explain: x depends only on price, not income, so the income effect on x is exactly 0 (the whole move is substitution).

q: Sam: u = x^0.75·y^0.25, m = 80, py = 4, px rises from 2 to 12. Marshallian x = 0.75·m/px falls from 30 to 5 (total −25). The HICKS substitution effect on x is closest to:
Same Sam problem (u = x^0.75·y^0.25, m = 80, py = 4, px 2→12, x0 = 30). The SLUTSKY substitution effect on x is:
Same Sam problem (total effect −25, SLUTSKY substitution effect −6.25). The Slutsky income effect on x is:
explain: Income effect = total − substitution = −25 − (−6.25) = −18.75.

q: A consumer buys 15 units of x. px rises from 4 to 6 and income is raised by exactly x·Δpx to keep the old bundle affordable (Slutsky). The raise is:
After a price rise, the substitution effect on an inferior good x is −4 and the income effect is +1. The total (Marshallian) effect is:
explain: Total = SE + IE = −4 + 1 = −3: still negative because the opposing income effect is small.

q: After a price rise the demand for x actually ROSE: the total effect is +1. If the substitution effect is −2, the income effect is:
explain: IE = total − SE = 1 − (−2) = +3; a positive income effect large enough to make x Giffen.

q: For good x a price rise gives substitution effect −5 and income effect −5 (normal), total −10. If instead the good were inferior with income effect +5, the total effect would become:
explain: Total = SE + IE = −5 + 5 = 0: the opposing income effect exactly cancels the substitution effect.

q: For x to be Giffen after a price rise with a substitution effect of −4, and the total effect turning out to be +2, the income effect must be:
explain: IE = total − SE = 2 − (−4) = +6: the income effect must more than offset the substitution effect.

q: u = x^(1/3)·y^(2/3), m = 90, py = 2, and px rises from 1 to 3. Marshallian x = m/(3·px). The TOTAL effect on x is:
explain: x = m/(3px): x falls from 90/3 = 30 to 90/9 = 10, a total effect of −20.

q: The Slutsky equation decomposes the total effect of a price change into:
explain: Total effect = substitution effect + income effect; this is the content of the Slutsky decomposition.
opts: the substitution effect plus the income effect
the substitution effect minus the income effect
the substitution effect times the income effect

q: A cinema raises its ticket price. Holding your utility fixed (Hicks compensation), the substitution effect alone makes you watch:
explain: Cinema is now relatively dearer; with utility fixed the substitution effect shifts you away from cinema toward the cheaper alternative.
opts: fewer cinema films and relatively more streaming
exactly the same mix as before
more of both cinema and streaming

q: Which (substitution effect, income effect) pair is possible for a NORMAL good whose price has just risen?
explain: For a price rise the substitution effect is negative; for a normal good the income effect is also negative, so both are negative.

q: For a price rise, the substitution effect and income effect point in the SAME direction (both reduce demand) exactly when the good is:
explain: For a normal good the income effect reinforces the (negative) substitution effect; inferior and Giffen goods have an opposing income effect.

q: The income effect points OPPOSITE to the substitution effect precisely when the good is:
explain: Inferior goods (Giffen is a special inferior case) have an income effect that opposes the substitution effect; normal goods reinforce it.

q: For a price RISE of a Giffen good, fill in: the substitution effect is ___ and the income effect is ___, with the income effect winning.
explain: The own substitution effect is always negative for a price rise; a Giffen good's positive (inferior) income effect outweighs it, so demand rises.

q: Bruno's cheap kibble is inferior (but not Giffen) and its price falls. The substitution effect raises his kibble; the income effect ___, and since kibble is inferior but not Giffen he ends up eating ___ kibble.
explain: A price fall raises real income and, for an inferior good, lowers kibble (opposing income effect); but the substitution effect dominates, so net kibble rises.

q: Compensated (Hicksian) demand is what you get when, at every price, income is adjusted to keep constant:
explain: Hicksian (compensated) demand holds utility fixed while prices vary; that is the defining feature of the substitution effect.

q: A uniform 30% rise in ALL prices, with utility held fixed, changes the Hicksian (compensated) bundle by:
explain: Hicksian demand is homogeneous of degree zero in prices: scaling all prices with utility fixed leaves the cost-minimizing bundle unchanged.
opts: nothing; Hicksian demand is homogeneous of degree zero in prices
an amount that cannot be signed

q: Two students compute the substitution effect of the same price fall, one via Slutsky and one via Hicks. They are guaranteed to agree on the ___ but generally not on the exact ___.
explain: Slutsky and Hicks substitution effects always share the same sign (opposite the price change) but generally differ in magnitude for a finite price change.

q: A hockey rink cuts its hourly fee. Holding an athlete's fitness (utility) fixed, the substitution effect shifts training time toward hockey because it is now relatively cheaper. This shift is:
explain: The own substitution effect never opposes a price fall, so with utility fixed the cheaper activity (hockey) weakly gains time.
opts: always toward hockey (the own substitution effect is non-negative for a price fall)
zero unless the two activities are perfect substitutes

q: Convex preferences mean the consumer values:
explain: Convex preferences mean the consumer values balance at least as much as extremes (averages ≽ extremes).
opts: balance at least as much as extremes

q: “Averages at least as good as extremes” defines:
explain: 'Averages at least as good as extremes' is the definition of convex preferences.

q: The MRS measures:
explain: The MRS is the amount of good 2 the consumer gives up for one more unit of good 1 at constant utility — the (absolute) slope of the indifference curve.
opts: how much x₂ you give up for one more x₁

q: Diminishing MRS: as x₁ rises you give up ____ x₂ per extra x₁:
explain: Diminishing MRS: as x₁ rises the consumer gives up less and less x₂ per extra x₁.

q: A diminishing MRS from left to right is a consequence of strict:
explain: A diminishing MRS (from left to right) is a consequence of strict convexity.

q: A and B equally good, preferences strictly convex; the midpoint M is:
explain: Strict convexity: if A and B are equally good and distinct, the midpoint M is strictly preferred to both.

q: Convexity is about the ____ of indifference curves:
explain: Convexity is a statement about the curvature (bowing) of indifference curves.

q: Convex indifference curves bow:
explain: Convex indifference curves bow toward the origin.

q: With very little x₁ and lots of x₂, your MRS (willingness to give up x₂ for x₁) is:
explain: With very little x₁ and lots of x₂, x₁ is scarce and valuable, so the consumer will give up a lot of x₂ for it — a large MRS.

q: Moving down-right along a convex curve, the slope gets:
explain: Moving down-right along a convex curve, diminishing MRS makes the slope flatter.

q: Perfect substitutes (straight-line ICs) are:
explain: Perfect substitutes have straight-line indifference curves: weakly convex with a constant MRS (not strictly convex).

q: Perfect complements (L-shaped ICs) are:
explain: Perfect complements (L-shaped curves) are weakly convex — the upper-contour set is convex but its boundary has straight arms, so they are not strictly convex.

q: Cobb-Douglas preferences u=xᵃ yᵇ are:
explain: Cobb-Douglas u=xᵃyᵇ (a,b greater than 0) is strictly convex: indifference curves bow strictly toward the origin with a strictly diminishing MRS.

q: Which guarantees a STRICTLY diminishing MRS:
explain: Only strict convexity guarantees a strictly diminishing MRS; weak convexity allows a constant MRS.

q: The exam says “strict” convexity for a diminishing MRS because weak convexity allows the MRS to be:
explain: The exam says 'strict' because weak convexity permits a constant MRS (perfect substitutes), which is not strictly diminishing.

q: The MRS of perfect substitutes is:
explain: The MRS of perfect substitutes is constant (straight-line indifference curves).

q: Straight-line indifference curves represent:
explain: Straight-line indifference curves represent perfect substitutes.

q: Preferences where extremes beat averages are:
explain: When extremes are preferred to averages, preferences are concave (non-convex).

q: At the kink of an L-shaped curve, the MRS is:
explain: At the kink of an L-shaped (perfect-complement) curve the slope, and hence the MRS, is undefined.

q: Which is convex but NOT strictly convex:
explain: Perfect substitutes are convex but NOT strictly convex (straight ICs, constant MRS); Cobb-Douglas forms — including √(xy) and x⁰·⁵y⁰·⁵ — are strictly convex.

q: Under convex preferences the set “at least as good as A” is:
explain: Convex preferences ⇔ the upper-contour set {at least as good as A} is a convex set.

q: A non-convex preference shows up as an upper-contour set with:
explain: A non-convex preference shows up as an upper-contour set with a dent (an inward notch).

q: “More is better” (the direction of improvement) is:
explain: 'More is better' — the direction of improvement — is monotonicity, not convexity.

q: Convexity is best described as being about:
explain: Convexity concerns the curvature of indifference curves (how they bow), not direction, prices or the number of goods.

q: Monotonic preferences:
explain: Monotonicity only fixes the direction of improvement; curvature is separate, so monotonic preferences may be convex or concave.

q: If the chord between two indifferent bundles lies on a HIGHER curve, preferences are:
explain: If the chord (average) between two indifferent bundles lies on a higher indifference curve, the average is preferred — convex preferences.

q: Concave (non-convex) preferences make the consumer prefer:
explain: Concave (non-convex) preferences make the consumer prefer corners/extremes over averages.

q: Convex preferences correspond to a utility function that is:
explain: Convex preferences correspond to a quasiconcave utility function (convex upper-contour sets).

q: Squaring a quasiconcave utility (a positive monotonic transform) leaves it:
explain: Squaring is a strictly increasing transform (for u ≥ 0); quasiconcavity is ordinal, so it is preserved. Verified: (xy)² has the same MRS y/x as xy, hence the same convex indifference map.

q: Strictly convex indifference curves:
explain: Strictly convex indifference curves have no flat (straight) segments — every mixture of two indifferent bundles is strictly better.

q: For u=xy, MRS = MUx/MUy =:
explain: For u=xy, MUx=y and MUy=x, so MRS = MUx/MUy = y/x.

q: For u=xy at (x,y)=(2,8), the MRS (=y/x) is:
explain: For u=xy, MRS = y/x; at (2,8) that is 8/2 = 4.

q: For u=xy at (x,y)=(8,2), the MRS is:
explain: For u=xy, MRS = y/x; at (8,2) that is 2/8 = 0.25.

q: Comparing those two, as x rises from 2 to 8 the MRS:
explain: MRS = y/x falls from 4 at (2,8) to 0.25 at (8,2): as x rises along the curve the MRS diminishes (convexity).

q: For perfect substitutes u=2x+y, the MRS is:
explain: For u=2x+y, MRS = MUx/MUy = 2/1 = 2, constant everywhere (perfect substitutes).

q: A constant MRS tells you the goods are:
explain: A constant MRS (straight-line curves) means the goods are perfect substitutes.

q: At an interior optimum with convex preferences, MRS equals:
explain: At an interior optimum the indifference curve is tangent to the budget line, so MRS = px/py.

q: With strictly convex preferences and a straight budget line, the optimum is:
explain: Strict convexity ensures the highest reachable indifference curve meets the budget line at exactly one point, so the optimum is unique (a tangency for smooth interior solutions, possibly a corner).

q: With concave (non-convex) preferences, the tangency point is:
explain: With concave (non-convex) preferences the tangency is the worst point; utility is maximised at a corner.
opts: the worst; the optimum is a corner

q: For u=x⁰·⁵y⁰·⁵ at (6,4), |MRS| = y/x =:
explain: For u=x⁰·⁵y⁰·⁵, |MRS| = y/x; at (6,4) that is 4/6 = 2/3. (The trap 1.5 is x/y.)

q: A utility function is quasiconcave if, for every level k, the set of bundles with u ≥ k is:
explain: Quasiconcavity means every upper-contour set {x: u(x) ≥ k} is convex — exactly the condition that preferences are convex (averages at least as good as extremes).

q: For u = x + y, bundles A = (4,0) and B = (0,4) are indifferent (u = 4). The average (2,2) gives utility:
explain: u(2,2) = 4 = u(A) = u(B): the midpoint is exactly as good as the extremes, not strictly better. This is why perfect substitutes are weakly convex but fail strict convexity.
opts: 4 — equally good, so preferences are weakly (not strictly) convex

q: With u = x² + y², bundles A = (4,0) and B = (0,4) are indifferent (u = 16). The average (2,2) gives u = 8, so the consumer:
explain: u(2,2) = 8 is less than 16: averaging makes this consumer worse off, so extremes beat averages. Preferences are concave (non-convex) and the optimum lies at a corner, not an interior tangency.
opts: prefers the extremes A or B — the optimum is a corner

q: Strict convexity of preferences guarantees that the utility-maximising bundle on a budget line is:
explain: Strictly convex (strictly quasiconcave) preferences make upper-contour sets strictly convex, so the highest attainable indifference curve touches the budget line at exactly one point — the optimum is unique.

q: If a consumer's preferences are concave (averages worse than extremes), the optimal choice is typically:
explain: Concave preferences make the tangency a minimum; utility is maximised by going to an extreme, so the optimum is a corner where the consumer spends everything on one good.
opts: a corner solution (all of one good)

q: For u = √(xy), compare the MRS (= y/x) at (1,4) and (4,1), both on the curve u = 2. Moving from (1,4) to (4,1) the MRS goes from:
explain: √(xy) has MRS = y/x. At (1,4) it is 4; at (4,1) it is 1/4. As x rises along the indifference curve (√(xy)=2 at both points) the MRS falls from 4 to 1/4 — diminishing MRS, confirming strict convexity.

q: Is u = x² + y² quasiconcave (does it represent convex preferences)?
explain: The set {(x,y): x²+y² ≥ k} is the region OUTSIDE a circle — a non-convex set — so u is not quasiconcave and preferences are non-convex (extremes beat averages). Being a convex function does not make a utility quasiconcave.
opts: No — its upper-contour sets are the outside of circles, which are non-convex
Yes — it is a sum of convex functions
Yes — it is a Cobb-Douglas form

q: Convexity is what makes the tangency condition MRS = px/py identify a utility MAXIMUM rather than a minimum, because:
explain: With convex (bowed-in) indifference curves, at the tangency the whole indifference curve lies on or above the budget line, so no affordable bundle is better — the tangency is a maximum. Without convexity the same tangency could be a minimum.
opts: the indifference curve bows toward the origin, staying on or above its tangent line

q: A strictly increasing transform of a concave utility function is always:
explain: Concavity is cardinal and can be destroyed by a monotone transform, but quasiconcavity (convex upper-contour sets) is ordinal and survives any strictly increasing transform. Since a concave function is quasiconcave, its increasing transforms stay quasiconcave.
opts: quasiconcave, though possibly no longer concave

q: Why do perfect substitutes u = x + y FAIL strict convexity?
explain: Strict convexity requires the mix of two distinct indifferent bundles to be STRICTLY preferred. On a straight-line indifference curve the mix stays on the same line (equally good), so only weak convexity holds: u(4,0)=u(0,4)=4 and u(2,2)=4, not greater.
opts: their ICs are straight lines, so a mix of two indifferent bundles is only equally good, not strictly better

q: Diminishing marginal rate of substitution is equivalent to indifference curves that are:
explain: A falling MRS as x rises means the curve flattens moving right — i.e. it bows toward the origin (convex to the origin). Diminishing MRS and convex-to-origin indifference curves are the same property.

q: “Averages are STRICTLY preferred to extremes” is the definition of:
explain: Strict convexity: for distinct indifferent bundles A and B, every strict mixture λA+(1−λ)B is strictly preferred to A and B. Weak convexity only requires 'at least as good'.

q: For u = min(x,y), bundles A = (2,4) and B = (2,6) both give u = 2. Their average (2,5) gives u = ___, showing min is convex but NOT strictly convex:
explain: min(2,5) = 2 = u(A) = u(B): along the vertical arm of the L, averaging gives no strict gain, so perfect complements are weakly but not strictly convex (the upper-contour set is convex but its boundary has straight segments).

q: A constant MRS (indifference curves are straight lines) tells you preferences are:
explain: Straight indifference lines (perfect substitutes) have a constant MRS; the average of two indifferent bundles is only equally good, so preferences are convex in the weak sense but fail strict convexity.
opts: weakly convex but not strictly convex

q: For u = x^(1/3) y^(2/3), the MRS = MUx/MUy simplifies to:
explain: MUx = (1/3)x^(−2/3)y^(2/3) and MUy = (2/3)x^(1/3)y^(−1/3); the ratio is (1/3)/(2/3)·(y/x) = y/(2x). It falls as x rises along a curve, so the MRS diminishes (strictly convex).

q: With perfect substitutes (weakly convex, straight ICs) and MRS ≠ px/py, the optimum is:
explain: Weak convexity does not force an interior solution. If the constant MRS differs from the price ratio, the consumer specialises in whichever good gives more utility per dollar — a corner. Only if MRS = px/py is the whole budget line optimal.
opts: a corner — all income on the good with more utility per dollar
the midpoint of the budget line

q: You are told u is quasiconcave. What does this imply about the consumer's preferences?
explain: Quasiconcave utility ⇔ convex upper-contour sets ⇔ convex preferences (averages at least as good as extremes). It does not by itself imply complements or non-satiation.
opts: they are convex — averages are at least as good as extremes
they are concave — extremes beat averages

q: u = xy is quasiconcave. Its strictly increasing transform v = (xy)³ is:
explain: v = g(u) with g(t)=t³ strictly increasing (for u ≥ 0), so v represents the same preferences; the MRS of (xy)³ is y/x, identical to u=xy, so the indifference map — and hence quasiconcavity — is unchanged.
opts: still quasiconcave — same indifference curves (MRS = y/x)

q: Which utility function represents preferences that are NOT convex?
explain: u = x²+y² has non-convex upper-contour sets (outside of circles) → concave preferences, extremes preferred. The other three are convex: √(xy) strictly, min(x,y) and x+y weakly. Check: average of (4,0),(0,4) gives 16 but midpoint (2,2) gives only 8.

q: Bruno the dog is equally happy with (4 treats, 0 belly-rubs) or (0 treats, 4 belly-rubs). If he STRICTLY prefers (2,2) to both, his preferences are:
explain: Strictly preferring the average (2,2) to two equally-liked extremes is exactly the definition of strict convexity (a taste for balance/variety).
opts: strictly convex — he likes a balanced mix

q: y is an economic bad, x is a good (x horizontal, y vertical). The indifference curves are:
explain: With one good (x) and one bad (y), MUx greater than 0 but MUy less than 0, so holding utility constant x and y must rise together: the indifference curve slopes upward.

q: Holding utility constant, if the consumer gets more of the bad y, staying equally content requires:
explain: More of the bad y lowers utility; to stay on the same indifference curve the consumer must be compensated with more of the good x.

q: With one good x and one bad y, moving in the direction “more good, less bad” (down-right) makes utility:
explain: Moving down-right means more good x and less bad y — both raise utility, so utility rises.

q: On the same upward-sloping map, the curve further to the lower-right (more x for the same y) represents:
explain: For a bad on the vertical axis, at the same y more x is better, so the curve lying further to the lower-right is the higher-utility one.

q: If y is a bad, then MU<sub>y</sub>=∂ U/∂ y is:
explain: A bad is defined by negative marginal utility: MUy = ∂U/∂y is less than 0.

q: A commuter's utility depends on income x (a good) and commute time y (a bad). To keep utility unchanged, an increase in commute time must be met with:
explain: Commute time y is a bad (MU less than 0); to hold utility fixed when it rises, income x (a good) must rise — a pay rise.

q: Bruno gets treats (x, a good) and baths (y, a bad). One more bath, to keep Bruno equally content, requires:
explain: Baths are a bad for Bruno, so one more bath must be offset by more treats (the good) to keep him equally content.

q: In the treats-and-baths diagram (treats horizontal, baths vertical), Bruno's indifference curves slope:
explain: Treats good and baths bad give an upward-sloping (positive-slope) indifference curve, like any good/bad pair.

q: For an ordinary good x<sub>2</sub> (not a bad), more x<sub>2</sub> holding x<sub>1</sub> fixed makes utility:
explain: An ordinary good has positive marginal utility, so more of it (holding the other fixed) raises utility.

q: On the mock exam Q6 diagram (y an economic bad, vertical; x horizontal), the curves are upward sloping, and moving right (more x, same y) makes utility:
explain: With the bad y on the vertical axis and the good x horizontal, curves slope upward and moving right (more x) increases utility.

q: Two ordinary goods x and y: the indifference curves slope:
explain: Two ordinary goods give the standard downward-sloping (negatively sloped) indifference curves.

q: With two ordinary goods, the direction of increasing utility points:
explain: With two goods, utility rises as you move away from the origin (up and to the right — more of both).

q: x is a good and y is a bad (x horizontal, y vertical). The direction of increasing utility points:
explain: x good and y bad: utility rises with more x and less y, i.e. toward the lower-right (down-right).

q: Two economic bads x and y (say, noise and pollution). The indifference curves slope:
explain: Two bads (noise, pollution) have MUx and MUy both less than 0, and the indifference curves slope downward.

q: With two bads, better bundles lie:
explain: With two bads, less of both is better, so preferred bundles lie down and to the left, toward the origin.
opts: down and to the left, toward the origin
up and to the left only

q: A student cares about study hours x (a bad, it is tiring) and grade y (a good), x horizontal, y vertical. The indifference curves slope:
explain: Study hours x is a bad (MUx less than 0), grade y a good (MUy greater than 0); slope dy/dx = −MUx/MUy is positive — upward sloping.

q: In the same setup (study hours x, a bad, horizontal; grade y, a good, vertical), the better bundles lie:
explain: Better means less study (less x) and a higher grade (more y): up and to the left.
opts: up and to the left (less study, higher grade)

q: Which case has indifference curves sloping downward AND improvement toward the origin:
explain: Downward-sloping curves with improvement toward the origin is the two-bads case.

q: Which case has indifference curves sloping downward AND improvement away from the origin:
explain: Downward-sloping curves with improvement away from the origin is the standard two-goods case.

q: A firm faces pollution fines x and cleanup delays y, both of which are bads. This is the case:
explain: Fines and delays are both bads → two-bads case: curves slope downward and welfare improves toward the origin.
opts: two goods, better away from the origin
one good, one bad, curves slope up
two bads, better toward the origin

q: With x a good and y a bad, MU<sub>x</sub>>0 and MU<sub>y</sub><0. The slope of the indifference curve, dy/dx=-MU<sub>x</sub>/MU<sub>y</sub>, is:
explain: Slope dy/dx = −MUx/MUy = −(positive)/(negative) = positive, so the indifference curve slopes upward.

q: If MU<sub>x</sub> and MU<sub>y</sub> have the same sign (both goods, or both bads), the slope -MU<sub>x</sub>/MU<sub>y</sub> is:
explain: If MUx and MUy share a sign (both goods or both bads), −MUx/MUy is negative: the curve slopes downward.

q: If exactly one of MU<sub>x</sub>,MU<sub>y</sub> is negative (one good, one bad), the ratio MU<sub>x</sub>/MU<sub>y</sub> is:
explain: If exactly one marginal utility is negative, MUx/MUy is negative (a positive divided by a negative, or vice versa).

q: When y is a bad, a negative value of MU<sub>x</sub>/MU<sub>y</sub> signals that the indifference curve, with x horizontal and y vertical, is:
explain: A negative MUx/MUy makes the slope −MUx/MUy positive, so with y a bad the curve slopes upward.

q: The relabelling trick for a bad y defines a new variable z equal to:
explain: Relabel the bad as its absence: z = M − y (for M large enough), which turns the bad into a good.
opts: the absence of the bad, e.g.\ z=M-y for a large enough M

q: After relabelling y (a bad) as z= absence of y (a good), the indifference curve in (x,z) becomes:
explain: In (x, z) with z = M − y a good, the map reverts to the standard downward-sloping shape.

q: Example: cleanliness z=10-dirt y, where dirt is a bad. After relabelling, a higher z means:
explain: z = 10 − dirt: a higher z means less dirt, and since dirt is a bad, less dirt raises utility.

q: Scenario: a factory's management utility depends on output x and noise complaints y; more complaints cost management its bonus. Here y is:
explain: Noise complaints reduce the manager's bonus (utility), so y has negative marginal utility — a bad.

q: Scenario: a runner's happiness depends on race medals x (a good) and recovery days needed y (unwelcome, a bad). With x horizontal and y vertical, the indifference curves are:
explain: Medals good and recovery days a bad give upward-sloping indifference curves.

q: In the runner scenario, moving down-right (more medals, fewer recovery days) makes the runner:
explain: More medals and fewer recovery days both help, so moving down-right makes the runner happier.

q: A consumer has u(x, y) = x − y², where x is a good. Evaluated at any y greater than 0, the marginal utility MUy = ∂u/∂y is:
explain: MUy = ∂u/∂y = −2y is less than 0 for y greater than 0. Negative marginal utility is exactly the definition of an economic bad.
opts: negative, so y is a bad
positive, so y is a good

q: For u(x, y) = 2√x − y (x a good, y a bad), the indifference-curve slope dy/dx = −MUx/MUy at x = 4 is:
explain: MUx = 1/√x and MUy = −1, so dy/dx = −MUx/MUy = −(1/√x)/(−1) = 1/√x. At x = 4 this is 1/2, greater than 0 — the curve slopes upward because y is a bad.

q: For u(x, y) = 3x − 2y (x a good, y a bad), the marginal rate of substitution MRS = MUx/MUy is:
explain: MUx = 3 and MUy = −2, so MRS = MUx/MUy = 3/(−2) = −3/2. A negative MRS is the signature of a good paired with a bad; the curve's slope −MRS = 3/2 is positive (upward).

q: Pollution y is a bad in u(x, y) = x − y. Define clean air z = M − y (M a large constant). The marginal utility of z, MUz = ∂u/∂z, is:
explain: Substituting y = M − z gives u = x − (M − z) = x + z − M, so MUz = ∂u/∂z = +1, greater than 0. Relabelling the bad as its absence turns it into an ordinary good with positive marginal utility.

q: A worker enjoys consumption x (a good) and dislikes noise y (a bad): u = x − y². Each extra unit of noise accepted raises pay by 10 units of x, so along the job offer x = 10y. The utility-maximising noise level y is:
explain: Substitute x = 10y: U(y) = 10y − y². Setting dU/dy = 10 − 2y = 0 gives y = 5 (with x = 50). This is an interior optimum trading the good off against the bad.

q: Both x and y are bads: u(x, y) = −x² − y². The indifference-curve slope dy/dx = −MUx/MUy at the point (1, 1) is:
explain: MUx = −2x and MUy = −2y, so dy/dx = −MUx/MUy = −(−2x)/(−2y) = −x/y = −1 at (1, 1). With two bads the curves slope downward and utility rises toward the origin (fewer of both).

q: An economic bad is best defined as a commodity whose:
explain: A bad is a good with negative marginal utility: consuming more reduces utility. Do not confuse it with an inferior good, which is defined by negative income elasticity.
opts: marginal utility is negative — more of it lowers utility

q: For a good, more is preferred to less. For a bad, the consumer prefers:
explain: Because marginal utility is negative, less of a bad is preferred to more; the direction of improvement points toward smaller quantities of the bad.

q: 'Hours worked' is unpleasant (a bad). Redefining the axis as leisure = 24 − hours worked makes leisure:
explain: Turning a bad into its absence (leisure = time not worked) flips the sign of marginal utility, so leisure is a good. This is the standard relabelling trick.
opts: a good, with positive marginal utility

q: Pollution is a bad, plotted on the vertical axis against a good x. If we instead plot 'clean air' = (maximum − pollution) on that axis, the indifference curves change from:
explain: With pollution (a bad) the curves slope upward; relabelling the axis as clean air (a good) restores the standard downward-sloping shape. Preferences are unchanged — only the description is.

q: With one good x and one bad y, the indifference curves slope upward. Can any of them slope downward?
explain: The slope −MUx/MUy with MUx greater than 0 and MUy less than 0 is positive everywhere, so the curves slope upward throughout — none can slope downward.
opts: No — while one is a good and the other a bad, the slope −MUx/MUy is positive

q: A consumer's utility is u = x − y with x a good and y a bad. If y can be chosen freely (it has no offsetting benefit), the optimum sets y at:
explain: Since MUy = −1 is less than 0, utility always rises as y falls, so the consumer drives the bad down to the lowest amount available — a corner solution. MUy is never 0 here, so there is no interior optimum.
opts: its lowest feasible level (a corner, e.g. y = 0)

q: With x a good and y a bad, the magnitude of the MRS (extra x needed to hold utility constant per extra unit of y) measures:
explain: Along an indifference curve, more of the bad y must be offset by more of the good x; the required extra x per unit of y is the compensation, i.e. |MRS|. The upward slope reflects exactly this trade-off.
opts: the compensation in the good needed to tolerate one more unit of the bad
the income effect of the bad

q: The marginal willingness to pay for one more unit of an economic bad is:
explain: Because the bad lowers utility, the consumer would accept more of it only in exchange for compensation, so marginal willingness to pay is negative.
opts: negative — the consumer must be paid to accept it

q: Bruno the dog's utility rises with treats (a good) and falls with nail-clipping sessions (a bad). Plotting treats horizontally and clippings vertically, a move straight up (more clippings, same treats) takes Bruno to:
explain: More of the bad (clippings) with no extra treats lowers utility, so Bruno drops to a lower indifference curve. Higher curves lie down and to the right (more treats, fewer clippings).

q: x is a good and y is a bad (x horizontal, y vertical). Relative to a given upward-sloping indifference curve, the strictly preferred bundles lie:
explain: Utility increases with more x and less y, i.e. toward the lower-right, so the better-than set sits below and to the right of any indifference curve.
opts: below and to the right (more x, less y)

q: A commodity y switches from being a good to being a bad (its marginal utility changes from positive to negative). The indifference-curve slope −MUx/MUy changes from:
explain: With y a good, MUy greater than 0 makes −MUx/MUy negative (downward). Once y becomes a bad, MUy less than 0 makes the slope positive (upward).

q: For two bads (say traffic noise and air pollution), which statement is correct?
explain: Both marginal utilities are negative, so −MUx/MUy is negative (downward-sloping), and less of either bad is better — utility rises toward the origin.
opts: Curves slope downward and utility rises toward the origin
Curves slope upward and utility rises away from the origin
Curves slope downward and utility rises away from the origin

q: Which statement correctly distinguishes an economic bad from an inferior good?
explain: A bad is defined by MU less than 0 (more is worse). An inferior good still has MU greater than 0 (more is better) but is bought less as income rises (η less than 0). The two concepts are unrelated.
opts: A bad has negative marginal utility; an inferior good has negative income elasticity but positive marginal utility
A bad has negative income elasticity; an inferior good has negative marginal utility

q: A footballer values goals x (a good) and dislikes yellow cards y (a bad). With goals horizontal and cards vertical, his indifference curves slope upward. A bundle with one extra goal and one fewer card is:
explain: More of the good and less of the bad both raise utility, so the new bundle is strictly preferred — it lies to the lower-right, on a higher indifference curve.

q: Relabelling a bad y as its absence z = M − y (a good) changes:
explain: The trick is a change of variable: the same bundles keep the same ranking. What changes is the picture — curves that sloped upward in (x, y) slope downward in (x, z).
opts: only the description/axis, not the underlying preferences
the consumer's actual ranking of bundles
the sign of MUx for the good
nothing at all, including the curve's slope in the diagram

q: A patient values health x (a good) and endures side-effects y (a bad) from a drug. On axes with x horizontal and y vertical, the indifference curves are:
explain: One good and one bad give slope −MUx/MUy = −(positive)/(negative), which is greater than 0, so the curves slope upward.

q: Among bundles on an upward-sloping indifference map (x a good, y a bad), the consumer most prefers the one that is:
explain: Utility increases with more x and less y, so the best reachable bundle lies as far to the lower-right as feasibility allows.
opts: farthest to the lower-right (most x, least y)

q: A consumer trades a good x against a bad y along an upward-sloping offer line (accepting more y buys more x). An interior optimum occurs where:
explain: As with ordinary tangency, the optimum sets the indifference-curve slope equal to the offer line's slope. Because y is a bad, both slopes are positive, and the tangency gives an interior trade-off between the good and the bad.
opts: the indifference curve is tangent to the offer line (slopes equal)
y is as small as possible
the offer line hits the vertical axis

q: Which combination gives UPWARD-sloping indifference curves?
explain: Upward slope requires −MUx/MUy greater than 0, i.e. MUx and MUy have opposite signs — exactly one good and one bad. Two goods or two bads give downward-sloping curves.
opts: exactly one of the two commodities is a bad
neither — indifference curves never slope up

q: A preference relation is called “rational” in consumer theory when it is:
explain: Rational preferences are defined by two axioms: completeness (any two bundles can be ranked) and transitivity (the rankings chain consistently).

q: Completeness of preferences means that for any two bundles A and B:
explain: Completeness means no pair is incomparable: for any A and B the consumer can say A is at least as good as B, or B at least as good as A (or both).
opts: the consumer can rank them: A at least as good as B, or B at least as good as A (or both)
A must be affordable whenever B is
A is always strictly better than B

q: Transitivity means that if A is at least as good as B, and B is at least as good as C, then:
explain: Transitivity: if A is at least as good as B and B at least as good as C, then A is at least as good as C — rankings pass along the chain.
opts: C must be strictly better than A
A and C cannot be compared
A is at least as good as C
B is worse than both A and C

q: If preferences are rational (complete and transitive), the choices they generate:
explain: Choices generated by maximizing rational (complete, transitive) preferences can never contradict themselves, so they must satisfy WARP.
opts: may or may not satisfy WARP depending on prices
satisfy WARP only when there are exactly two goods

q: Why does transitivity rule out a cyclical choice pattern such as “A over B, B over C, C over A” when every pair is ranked?
explain: Transitivity forces one consistent ordering, so a cycle like A over B over C over A is impossible — no bundle can be ranked worse than itself.
opts: transitivity forces a consistent ranking, so no bundle can end up worse than itself
transitivity does not restrict cycles at all

q: Rational preferences guarantee that observed choices are:
explain: Rational preferences yield a single consistent ranking, so observed choices show no pairwise reversals.
opts: internally consistent, with no pairwise reversals

q: Which pair of properties, together, is the textbook definition of “rational preferences” used in this course?
explain: The textbook definition of rational preferences in this course is exactly completeness plus transitivity.

q: A consumer strictly prefers A to B, B to C, and also strictly prefers C to A (every pair is ranked). These preferences are:
explain: Strict cycle A over B, B over C, C over A ranks every pair (so it is complete) but breaks the chaining requirement, so it is complete but not transitive.

q: Suppose a data set of choices satisfies WARP. Can we conclude the underlying preferences are rational in the strongest (SARP) sense, guaranteed free of any longer inconsistent cycle?
explain: WARP only forbids two-way (pairwise) contradictions; a data set can pass WARP yet still contain a longer inconsistent cycle that only SARP rules out.
opts: not necessarily; WARP only rules out two-way (pairwise) contradictions, not longer cycles
yes, always, regardless of how many observations there are
no, WARP actually implies the preferences are non-convex
yes, but only if the consumer has intransitive preferences

q: The logical relationship “rational preferences imply WARP” means that:
explain: Rational preferences imply WARP: completeness and transitivity force WARP-consistent choices, but WARP alone does not prove full rationality (the converse is not automatic).
opts: WARP alone is sufficient to prove preferences are fully rational
completeness and transitivity together force the choices to satisfy WARP, though the converse is not automatic
WARP and rationality are unrelated conditions
WARP implies transitivity but not completeness

q: A classmate claims: “rational preferences can sometimes generate choices that fail WARP, in edge cases like indifference.” This claim is:
explain: The claim is incorrect: rational preferences must always generate WARP-consistent choices, with no exception, even under indifference.
opts: correct, but only with more than two goods
incorrect; rational preferences must generate WARP-consistent choices, with no exception
correct, only under decreasing marginal utility

q: Under budget line 2, is bundle a=(2,6) affordable?
explain: Bundle a=(2,6) is not affordable on budget line 2: its cost (about 6.67) exceeds the income of 4, so it lies outside that budget set.
opts: no, its cost of about 6.67 exceeds the income of 4

q: Under budget line 1, is bundle b=(3,3) affordable?
explain: Bundle b=(3,3) costs 3+3=6, which is within the income of 8 on budget line 1, so it is affordable.
opts: yes, it costs 3+3=6, within the income of 8
only if x and y are measured in the same units

q: Given that a was chosen while b was affordable (under budget line 1), and b was chosen only when a was NOT affordable (under budget line 2), this choice pattern:
explain: a is chosen when b is affordable, but b is chosen only when a is NOT affordable, so the situation that would create a contradiction never arises — consistent with WARP.
opts: violates WARP because a and b were both chosen
violates WARP because b is cheaper than a
cannot be evaluated without a utility function
is fully consistent with WARP; there is no contradiction

q: The pattern above does not violate WARP because:
explain: No WARP violation: because a is unaffordable under budget line 2, we never have b chosen while a is affordable, so the two-way contradiction cannot occur.
opts: a is not affordable under budget line 2, so the situation needed for a contradiction, namely b chosen while a is affordable, never arises
bundle b is strictly preferred to bundle a
budget line 1 lies entirely inside budget line 2

q: Under budget line 1, is bundle b=(2,5.6) affordable?
explain: Bundle b=(2,5.6) costs 2+5.6=7.6, within the income of 8 on budget line 1, so it is affordable.
opts: yes, it costs 2+5.6=7.6, within the income of 8
no, because b was chosen under budget line 2

q: Under budget line 2, is bundle a=(6,2) affordable?
explain: Bundle a=(6,2) costs 0.7·6+2=6.2, within the income of 7 on budget line 2, so it is affordable.
opts: yes, it costs 0.7(6)+2=6.2, within the income of 7
no, because a was chosen under budget line 1

q: Given the results of Q5 and Q6, this choice pattern:
explain: Here a was chosen while b was affordable AND b was chosen while a was affordable, giving contradictory revealed preferences — a WARP violation.
opts: is consistent because each bundle was chosen on its own budget line
cannot be evaluated because the budget lines cross
is consistent because a and b are different bundles
violates WARP: a was chosen while b was affordable, and b was chosen while a was affordable

q: The deep reason the pattern in Q5 to Q7 is a genuine WARP violation is that:
explain: The pattern reveals both a preferred to b and b preferred to a at the same time, which is the defining contradiction WARP forbids.
opts: it shows two contradictory revealed preferences, “a preferred to b” and “b preferred to a”, holding at the same time
the budget lines have different intercepts
bundle a contains more of good x than bundle b

q: A violation of WARP such as the one in Q7 implies that the observed choices:
explain: A WARP violation cannot come from any rational (complete, transitive) preference relation, because such preferences always generate consistent choices.
opts: were generated by strictly convex preferences
cannot have been generated by any rational (well-behaved) preference relation
must involve an error in the experimenter's data entry
are still consistent with some transitive preference ordering

q: On a diagram with two crossing budget lines, a WARP violation typically looks like:
explain: A typical WARP violation on crossing budget lines has each chosen bundle lying beyond the crossing point, so each was also affordable under the other budget.
opts: both chosen bundles lying on the same budget line
the chosen bundle always at a corner
each chosen bundle lying beyond the crossing point, so it was also affordable under the other budget line
the two budget lines never touching

q: If instead bundle a=(6,2) had NOT been affordable under budget line 2 (its cost exceeded 7), then the choice of b would:
explain: If a is not affordable when b is chosen, the two-way contradiction cannot form, so there is no WARP violation.
opts: still be a WARP violation regardless
no longer create a contradiction, since a WARP violation requires that each bundle be affordable when the other is chosen

q: If a consumer chooses bundle A when bundle B is also affordable, we say that:
explain: Choosing A while B is affordable means A is directly revealed preferred to B — the basic definition of revealed preference.
opts: B is directly revealed preferred to A
A is directly revealed preferred to B

q: Revealed preference theory recovers information about preferences by:
explain: Revealed preference recovers preference information purely from observed choices under different budgets, without assuming any cardinal utility number.
opts: assuming a specific utility function from the start
surveying the consumer directly about their tastes
measuring marginal utility in a laboratory
observing actual choices made under different budgets, without needing to assume any utility number

q: If A is directly revealed preferred to B, and B is directly revealed preferred to C, then A is said to be:
explain: If A is directly revealed preferred to B and B directly revealed preferred to C, then A is indirectly revealed preferred to C by chaining.
opts: directly revealed preferred to C only if there are two goods

q: The Strong Axiom of Revealed Preference (SARP) differs from WARP mainly in that SARP:
explain: SARP strengthens WARP by also ruling out longer inconsistent cycles, using the full chain of revealed preference rather than single pairs.
opts: also rules out longer inconsistent cycles, using the full chain of revealed preference, not just single pairs

q: WARP is best described as ruling out:
explain: WARP rules out the direct two-way contradiction: A revealed preferred to B and then B revealed preferred to A.
opts: any cycle of any length among revealed preferences
a direct two-way contradiction: A revealed preferred to B, and then B revealed preferred to A

q: SARP is needed, beyond WARP, in order to:
explain: SARP is what is needed to fully rationalize a data set with a complete, transitive preference relation, because it also excludes longer cycles.
opts: fully rationalize a data set of choices with a well-behaved (complete, transitive) preference relation, including ruling out longer cycles

q: A choice pattern that violates WARP:
explain: A choice pattern that violates WARP cannot have been generated by any rational preference relation, convex or not.
opts: cannot have been generated by any rational (complete and transitive) preference relation
can still be generated by some rational preference relation, just not a convex one
only affects the SARP test, not the underlying rationality
implies the consumer has incomplete but possibly transitive preferences

q: The practical value of revealed preference theory, for testing demand behavior empirically, is that it lets economists:
explain: The practical power of revealed preference is testing the consistency of observed choices without ever assuming or estimating a cardinal utility function.
opts: directly measure utils from survey data
test the consistency of observed choices without ever having to assume or estimate a cardinal utility function
prove that all consumers have convex preferences
replace budget constraints with indifference curves

q: Suppose A is directly revealed preferred to B, and separately C is directly revealed preferred to A. Then, by the logic used to build SARP, we can say C is:
explain: From A directly revealed preferred to B and C directly revealed preferred to A, chaining gives C indirectly revealed preferred to B.

q: Which statement correctly ranks the two axioms by strength?
explain: SARP is at least as strong as WARP: it requires WARP for every pair plus consistency across longer chains.
opts: SARP and WARP are always exactly equivalent, for any number of goods
neither axiom is ever related to the other
SARP is at least as strong as WARP: SARP requires WARP to hold for every pair, plus consistency across longer chains

q: Jane buys 12 kg potatoes + 6 kg beef; p_pot=10, p_beef=250. Beef rises to 350. Slutsky income compensation? [Δp·old q = 100·6]
explain: Slutsky compensation gives the consumer just enough extra income to still afford the OLD bundle at the new prices: Δincome = Δp·(old quantity) = (350−250)·6 = 600.

q: Price of good 2 rises, purchasing power (Slutsky) held constant. The new bundle has good 1 lower than x1¹ only if:
explain: Preserved verified key. Holding Slutsky purchasing power fixed isolates the substitution move; good 1 ends up below its reference level only through a negative (inferior-good) income response, i.e. when good 1 is inferior.
a: Good 1 is inferior.

q: Rational, monotonic, strictly convex prefs; p2 rises, purchasing power held constant. Then the compensated bundle has:
explain: With rational, monotonic, strictly convex preferences the pure substitution (Slutsky) effect of a rise in p2 shifts the compensated bundle toward the now-relatively-cheaper good 1 and away from good 2: more good 1, less good 2.
a: More of good 1 and less of good 2 than the initial bundle.

q: If a consumer has rational preferences, then his choice:
explain: Rational (complete, transitive) preferences generate choices that satisfy both WARP and SARP.
a: Must satisfy WARP and SARP.

q: Clothing price +10%, food +5%; before the change food was 80% of the budget and clothing 20%. Consumer Price Index (Laspeyres)? [0.8·1.05+0.2·1.10]
explain: A Laspeyres-type CPI weights the price relatives by base-period budget shares: 0.8·1.05 + 0.2·1.10 = 1.06.

q: William: London (6 fish&chips, 6 pizza; p=6,7) → Liverpool (10 fish&chips, 0 pizza; p=2,5). Which is true?
explain: At London prices (6,7) the London bundle (6,6) costs 78 while the Liverpool bundle (10,0) costs 60 ≤ 78, so London is directly revealed preferred to Liverpool. At Liverpool prices (2,5) the London bundle costs 42 greater than the Liverpool cost 20, so it was not affordable — no contradiction, no WARP violation.
a: The London bundle is directly revealed preferred to the Liverpool bundle, and there is no evidence he violates WARP.

q: Prices of ALL goods double. Which is true?
explain: When every price scales by the same factor, the Laspeyres index equals that factor exactly (no substitution to bias it): all prices doubling gives an index of 2, measuring the cost-of-living change precisely.
a: The Laspeyres price index measures the change in the cost of living precisely (=2).

q: Mustafa: Algeria p=(4,3) bundle (5,4); Burundi p=(3,5) bundle (4,6); Congo bundle (1,8). Which is true?
explain: Burundi (3,5)·bundle(4,6)=42 and Algeria bundle (5,4) costs 35 ≤ 42, so Burundi is revealed preferred to Algeria; Algeria (4,3)·bundle(5,4)=32 and Congo (1,8) costs 28 ≤ 32, so Algeria is revealed preferred to Congo. Congo costs 43 greater than 42 at Burundi prices, so the Burundi-to-Congo link is only INDIRECT (via Algeria).
a: The Burundian bundle is indirectly revealed preferred to the Congo bundle.

q: Larry chooses A=(8,6), p1=4, p2=7 (spends all income = 74). A is directly revealed preferred to which of (15,2),(7,8),(2,10)?
explain: Larry's income is 4·8+7·6=74. Bundle (15,2) costs 4·15+7·2=74 ≤ 74, so it was affordable when A was chosen and A is directly revealed preferred to it. The others cost 84 and 78, both above 74.
a: (15,2) — it costs 4·15+7·2=74 ≤ 74, so it was affordable when A was chosen.

q: Consumer chooses x when y affordable, and y when z affordable, and choices satisfy SARP. Then if z is chosen:
explain: Under SARP, x is (indirectly) revealed preferred to z through the chain x→y→z, so if z is chosen neither x nor y may be affordable — otherwise z would be revealed preferred to something ranked above it, a forbidden cycle.
a: Neither x nor y can be affordable.

q: A consumer picks bundle A when bundle B lies within the same budget. We conclude:
explain: Choosing A when B was affordable directly reveals A as at least as good as B: A is directly revealed preferred to B.
opts: B is directly revealed preferred to A
A is directly revealed preferred to B

q: The Weak Axiom of Revealed Preference says that:
explain: WARP forbids a two-way contradiction: you cannot have both A revealed preferred to B and B revealed preferred to A.
opts: every affordable bundle is chosen at least once
if A is revealed preferred to B, then B is never revealed preferred to A

q: At prices (px, py) = (3, 2) a consumer spends all income on the bundle (4, 5). Is the bundle (6, 1) revealed inferior to what she chose?
explain: Income is 3·4+2·5 = 22. Bundle (6,1) costs 3·6+2·1 = 20 ≤ 22, so it was affordable and her chosen bundle is directly revealed preferred to it.
opts: no, (6,1) costs more than her income
yes, (6,1) costs 20 which is within her income of 22, so her choice is revealed preferred to it
yes, but only if (6,1) is cheaper per unit

q: Observation 1: at prices (2, 1) the consumer buys (4, 1). Observation 2: at prices (1, 2) she buys (1, 4). Do these choices violate WARP?
explain: Both incomes are 9. Bundle (1,4) costs 2·1+1·4 = 6 ≤ 9 in observation 1, and (4,1) costs 1·4+2·1 = 6 ≤ 9 in observation 2, so each is affordable when the other is chosen — a WARP violation.
opts: yes: each bundle was affordable when the other was chosen, so both are revealed preferred to each other

q: Observation 1: at prices (1, 2) the consumer buys (6, 3). Observation 2: at prices (2, 1) she buys (3, 6). Are these choices consistent with WARP?
explain: Both incomes are 12. Bundle (3,6) costs 1·3+2·6 = 15 greater than 12 in observation 1, and (6,3) costs 2·6+1·3 = 15 greater than 12 in observation 2, so neither is affordable when the other is chosen — fully consistent with WARP.
opts: no, they always violate WARP when budgets cross
yes: neither bundle was affordable when the other was chosen, so no contradiction can arise

q: A data set shows A revealed preferred to B, B revealed preferred to C, and C revealed preferred to A. This three-step cycle:
explain: SARP forbids any revealed-preference cycle; a closed loop A→B→C→A is exactly the kind of longer inconsistency SARP rules out.
opts: violates SARP (and hence cannot come from rational preferences)

q: How does SARP go beyond WARP?
explain: WARP only bans pairwise reversals; SARP additionally bans longer cycles by chaining the full revealed-preference relation.
opts: it applies only to two goods
it rules out longer revealed-preference cycles, not just direct two-way reversals

q: If A is directly revealed preferred to B and B is directly revealed preferred to C, then with respect to C, A is:
explain: Chaining two direct revealed preferences gives an INDIRECT revealed preference: A is indirectly revealed preferred to C.

q: Revealed preference lets us bound an unobserved indifference curve because:
explain: Recoverability: bundles revealed preferred to x are at least as good as x, and bundles x is revealed preferred to are no better, so the true indifference curve through x is bounded between these sets.
opts: bundles revealed preferred to x lie on it
bundles revealed preferred to x must be at least as good, and bundles to which x is revealed preferred must be no better, sandwiching the indifference set
the budget line is the indifference curve

q: At base prices (2, 3) the consumer chose the base bundle (4, 2). The later bundle (3, 1) costs 9 at those base prices, below the base spending of 14. This tells us:
explain: The later bundle was affordable when the base bundle was chosen (9 ≤ 14), so the base bundle is revealed preferred to it — equivalently the Laspeyres quantity index (p⁰·q¹)/(p⁰·q⁰) = 9/14 is below 1.
opts: the later bundle is revealed preferred to the base bundle
the base bundle is directly revealed preferred to the later bundle, matching a Laspeyres quantity index below 1

q: At current prices (1, 4) the consumer chose (6, 1). The earlier bundle (2, 2) costs 10 at current prices, equal to the current spending of 10. This means:
explain: The earlier bundle was affordable at current prices (10 ≤ 10), so the current bundle is revealed preferred to it — equivalently the Paasche quantity index (p¹·q¹)/(p¹·q⁰) = 10/10 is at least 1.
opts: the earlier bundle is revealed preferred to the current one
the current bundle is revealed preferred to the earlier bundle, matching a Paasche quantity index of at least 1

q: Bruno the dog is offered treat A and treat B; he can reach both but grabs A. In revealed-preference terms:
explain: He chose A when B was equally available (affordable), so A is directly revealed preferred to B.
opts: B is revealed preferred to A
A is directly revealed preferred to B, since B was available and he chose A

q: Observation 1: at prices (3, 1) the consumer buys (5, 2). Observation 2: at prices (1, 3) she buys (2, 5). Is this a WARP violation?
explain: Both incomes equal 17. Bundle (2,5) costs 3·2+1·5 = 11 ≤ 17 in observation 1, and (5,2) costs 1·5+3·2 = 11 ≤ 17 in observation 2, so each was affordable when the other was chosen — a WARP violation.
opts: no, the incomes differ so it cannot be judged
yes: with both incomes equal to 17, each bundle was affordable when the other was chosen
no, because the bundles are symmetric

q: A consumer with income 20 buys (5, 5) at prices (2, 2). Which bundle is directly revealed inferior to her choice?
explain: Her choice is directly revealed preferred to any affordable bundle. (8,1) costs 2·8+2·1 = 18 ≤ 20 (affordable); the others cost 22 and 24, above her income.
opts: (8, 1), which costs 18 and was therefore affordable
none, since she spent all her income

q: The chief methodological advantage of revealed preference is that it:
explain: Revealed preference works entirely from observed price-quantity data and needs no cardinal utility, letting economists test consistency directly.
opts: tests choice consistency using only observed prices and quantities, with no cardinal utility assumed
assumes a Cobb-Douglas utility from the start

q: If A is (directly or indirectly) revealed preferred to B, SARP requires that:
explain: SARP forbids reversing any established revealed preference: if A is revealed preferred to B, then B cannot be revealed preferred to A, ruling out cycles.
opts: B may still be revealed preferred to A
B is never revealed preferred to A, so no cycle forms
A is affordable whenever B is

q: From two observations we learn that bundle x is revealed preferred to y, and z is revealed preferred to x. The recoverable ranking places:
explain: Revealed preference chains: z is revealed preferred to x and x to y, so the recovered ranking is z at least as good as x at least as good as y.
opts: z at least as good as x, and x at least as good as y

q: If one budget line lies entirely inside another (same prices, less income), then comparing the two chosen bundles:
explain: With nested budgets only one direction of affordability holds, so the two-way contradiction WARP forbids cannot occur — no violation is possible.
opts: cannot violate WARP, because a bundle affordable on the inner budget is affordable on the outer one but not conversely

q: A fan can afford either 90 minutes of football or 90 minutes of hockey and picks football. This choice:
explain: Football was chosen when hockey was equally affordable, so football is directly revealed preferred to hockey.
opts: directly reveals football preferred to hockey, since hockey was affordable and football was chosen

q: Observation 1: at prices (1, 1) with income 10 the consumer buys (8, 2). Observation 2: at prices (1, 2) with income 10 she buys (4, 3). Are the choices consistent with WARP?
explain: In observation 1, (4,3) costs 7 ≤ 10 so the first bundle is revealed preferred to it. In observation 2, (8,2) costs 1·8+2·2 = 12 greater than 10, so it was not affordable and no reverse revelation occurs — consistent with WARP.
opts: yes: bundle (4,3) was affordable in observation 1 so it is revealed inferior, and (8,2) was not affordable in observation 2, so no reversal occurs

q: A choice pattern can satisfy WARP yet still fail SARP when:
explain: WARP checks only pairs; a data set with no pairwise reversal can still hide a longer revealed-preference cycle that only SARP detects.
opts: no pair is directly contradictory but a longer chain forms a cycle (A→B→C→A)

q: Which ranking of the two axioms by logical strength is correct?
explain: SARP implies WARP and adds the no-longer-cycles requirement, so SARP is at least as strong as WARP.
opts: WARP is strictly stronger than SARP
SARP is at least as strong as WARP: it implies WARP plus consistency over longer chains
they are always equivalent for any data

q: Because a rational consumer's choices satisfy revealed preference, the compensated (Slutsky) own-price demand response must be:
explain: Revealed preference implies the Slutsky compensated own-price effect is non-positive — the compensated demand curve cannot slope up.
opts: non-positive: revealed preference implies the compensated demand for a good does not rise when its own price rises

q: In the endowment model the consumer's budget constraint is:
explain: In the endowment model money income is the market value of the endowment, so the budget is p1x1+p2x2 = p1ω1+p2ω2.
opts: p<sub>1</sub>x<sub>1</sub>+p<sub>2</sub>x<sub>2</sub>=M for a fixed money income M

q: The budget line always passes through:
explain: Consuming exactly the endowment costs p1ω1+p2ω2, precisely its value, so ω always satisfies the budget equation.
opts: the midpoint between the two axis intercepts

q: Why does the line always pass through ω?
explain: Buying exactly the endowment costs exactly what the endowment is worth, so ω is affordable at every price vector.
opts: consuming exactly ω costs exactly what you own, so it is affordable at any price
the consumer is forced to hold ω
ω is always the utility-maximising bundle

q: The slope of the endowment budget line is:
explain: Rewriting p1x1+p2x2 = constant gives x2 = const minus (p1/p2)x1, a slope of minus p1/p2.

q: If p<sub>1</sub> falls, p<sub>2</sub> fixed, the line:
explain: The line always passes through ω; a lower p1 makes the slope minus p1/p2 less steep, so it pivots about ω and flattens.
opts: shifts outward keeping the same slope

q: In the FIXED-MONEY-INCOME model instead, a fall in p<sub>1</sub> pivots the line around:
explain: With fixed money income M the vertical intercept M/p2 is unchanged, so a fall in p1 swings the x1-intercept out, pivoting about the x2-intercept M/p2.

q: The endowment income I=p<sub>1</sub>ω<sub>1</sub>+p<sub>2</sub>ω<sub>2</sub> is:
explain: I = p1ω1+p2ω2 is the market value of the endowment, so it changes when prices change.
opts: a function of prices: the market value of what you own

q: At the bundle x=ω itself, the consumer is:
explain: Consuming exactly the endowment means zero net trade in every good.
opts: at the utility-maximising bundle for sure
neither a net buyer nor a net seller of anything

q: If p<sub>1</sub> rises, p<sub>2</sub> fixed, the new line:
explain: A higher p1 steepens the slope minus p1/p2 while ω stays affordable, so the line pivots about ω and becomes steeper.

q: Two different endowments with the same market value at the same prices trace:
explain: The budget line depends only on prices and the endowment's total value p1ω1+p2ω2; equal value at equal prices gives the identical line.
opts: lines that cross only at the origin

q: Points on the budget line to the right of ω (more x<sub>1</sub> than ω<sub>1</sub>) are bundles where, if chosen, the consumer is:
explain: A point to the right of ω has x1 greater than ω1, i.e. she is buying good 1 on net.

q: A consumer is a net buyer of good 1 if:
explain: A net buyer consumes more than she owns: x1* greater than ω1.

q: A consumer is a net seller of good 2 if:
explain: A net seller consumes less than she owns: x2* less than ω2, selling the difference.

q: With exactly two goods, a strict net buyer of good 1 must (by the budget constraint) be:
explain: The budget through ω forces p1(x1 minus ω1) = minus p2(x2 minus ω2); buying good 1 on net makes the left side positive, so she must sell good 2 on net.
opts: a strict net seller of good 2
also a strict net buyer of good 2

q: A net buyer of good 1 is made BETTER off by:
explain: A net buyer of good 1 gains when the good she buys gets cheaper.

q: A net buyer of good 1 is made WORSE off by:
explain: A net buyer of good 1 is hurt when the good she buys gets more expensive.
opts: a rise in her own endowment ω<sub>1</sub>

q: A net seller of good 2 is made BETTER off by:
explain: A net seller of good 2 gains when the good she sells gets dearer.

q: A net seller of good 2 is made WORSE off by:
explain: A net seller of good 2 is hurt when the good she sells gets cheaper.

q: The mirror rule: a net buyer gains when the price of the good she buys ____ ; a net seller gains when the price of the good she sells ____ .
explain: A net buyer gains when the price she pays falls; a net seller gains when the price she receives rises.

q: A renter who owns no housing at all is a net ____ of housing services; a fall in rent makes her ____ .
explain: Owning no housing makes her a pure net buyer of housing services, so a rent (price) fall makes her better off.

q: A farmer sells eggs and buys wheat. A fall in the price of wheat makes the farmer:
explain: The farmer is a net buyer of wheat, so a fall in the wheat price makes her better off.
opts: worse off, only if she also sells wheat

q: If a net buyer of good 1 sees p<sub>1</sub> fall, her utility:
explain: A net buyer of good 1 is made better off by a fall in p1, so her utility rises.
opts: is impossible to sign without more information

q: By the WARP-style argument, a consumer who is a net buyer of good 1, after p<sub>1</sub> FALLS, will:
explain: Revealed preference rules out flipping to a net seller after a fall in the price of the good she buys, except at the knife-edge x1=ω1.
opts: generally become a net seller of good 1
remain a net buyer of good 1 (except possibly at a knife-edge)
become a net buyer of good 2 instead
always end up exactly at x<sub>1</sub><sup>*</sup>=ω<sub>1</sub>

q: The first step of the argument shows that, after p<sub>1</sub> falls, the OLD optimal bundle x<sup>*</sup>:
explain: A net buyer has x1* greater than ω1 (right of ω); after p1 falls the flatter line lies above the old one there, so x* is strictly inside the new budget set.
opts: is strictly affordable under the new budget, with income to spare
costs exactly the new income, no more no less

q: Since x<sup>*</sup> is strictly inside the new budget set, the new optimal bundle must be:
explain: Because x* is strictly interior to the new budget set she can afford something strictly better, so the new optimum is strictly preferred to x*.

q: The second step asks whether a hypothetical net-seller bundle (x<sub>1</sub>'<sup>*</sup>≤ω<sub>1</sub>), priced at the OLD prices, would have been:
explain: A would-be net-seller bundle (x1' at most ω1) valued at the OLD prices turns out weakly affordable then, contradicting x* having been the best choice at the old prices.
opts: (weakly) affordable at the old prices, conflicting with x<sup>*</sup> having been the best choice back then

q: The contradiction that rules out becoming a net seller is:
explain: Assuming she becomes a net seller forces x* to be both strictly better than and weakly worse than the same bundle, which is impossible.
opts: prices would have to be negative
x<sup>*</sup> would have to be simultaneously strictly better than, and weakly worse than, the hypothetical seller bundle
the budget line would skip ω

q: The one case the argument cannot rule out is the knife-edge one, where the consumer ends up:
explain: The only case not ruled out is landing exactly on the endowment, x1=ω1, trading nothing at the margin.
opts: at a corner solution with x<sub>2</sub>=0
exactly at x<sub>1</sub>'<sup>*</sup>=ω<sub>1</sub>: trading nothing at the margin

q: In the fixed-income Slutsky equation the income term has coefficient -x<sub>1</sub>. In the endowment model this coefficient becomes:
explain: With an endowment the money income p1ω1+p2ω2 moves with p1, so the income coefficient changes from minus x1 to (ω1 minus x1).

q: This extra term exists because, in the endowment model:
explain: Only in the endowment model does income I=p1ω1+p2ω2 change with p1, which adds the endowment-income term.

q: For a net buyer of good 1 (x<sub>1</sub>>ω<sub>1</sub>) with a normal good, the endowment-income term (ω<sub>1</sub>-x<sub>1</sub>) ∂ x<sub>1</sub>/∂ m is:
explain: For a net buyer ω1 minus x1 is negative and dx1/dm is positive, so the endowment-income term is negative and reinforces the negative substitution effect.
opts: positive, and can make demand slope upward

q: For a net SELLER of good 1 (x<sub>1</sub><ω<sub>1</sub>) with a normal good, this same term is:
explain: For a net seller ω1 minus x1 is positive and dx1/dm is positive, so the term is positive and can outweigh the substitution effect: the mechanism behind backward-bending labour supply.
opts: irrelevant, sellers have no income effect
positive, and can in principle outweigh the substitution effect: the mechanism behind backward-bending labor supply

q: Milton endowed with 35 x and 20 y; px=5, py=7. Maximum quantity of x he can consume? [sell all y: (35·5+20·7)/5]
explain: Selling his whole endowment yields 35*5+20*7 = 315; all spent on x at px=5 buys 315/5 = 63.

q: Lucy: px=4, py=6, endowment 8 x and A units of y. NET demand for x is 3, GROSS demand for y is 10. Find A. [budget through endowment]
explain: Net demand for x is 3 so x*=11; gross y*=10. Budget through the endowment 4*11+6*10 = 4*8+6*A gives A = 12.

q: John: u=xy, endowed with 76 x and no y; px=4, py=1. His NET demand for y? [optimum x*=38 ⇒ y*=152, net y = 152−0]
explain: Income = 4*76 = 304; Cobb-Douglas u=xy spends half on y so y*=304/(2*1)=152, and owning no y makes net demand for y = 152.

q: Lara: perfect substitutes (indifferent between x and y), endowment 8 x and 15 y; p_y = 3·p_x. Units of x she consumes? [sell y for x: 8+15·3]
explain: With px less than py, perfect substitutes hold only x; selling all y buys 15*(py/px)=15*3=45 units, plus the 8 owned gives 53.

q: Jake: endowment (6,6), plans (5,8). Price of y falls, px fixed. His initial bundle (5,8):
explain: The budget pivots about the endowment (6,6); Jake was a net buyer of y, and after py falls his old bundle (5,8) is still affordable but no longer optimal.
a: Is still available and NOT optimal (the budget pivots around the endowment, opening better bundles).

q: James: px=4, py=6, endowment (10,10), plans (12,8). Prices change to px=6, py=9. Then he is:
explain: New prices (6,9) = 1.5*(4,6) scale income too, leaving the budget line unchanged, so he is neither better nor worse off.
a: Neither better off nor worse off (new prices proportional to the old direction through the endowment value).

q: Endowment (5,8)→(8,7), same prices (px=4, py=7). After the endowment change:
explain: Same prices mean only endowment value matters: it rises from 4*5+7*8=76 to 4*8+7*7=81, a pure income increase, so an inferior x has lower gross demand.
a: If x is an inferior good, gross demand for x decreases.

q: Bill: endowment (10,10), plans (8,14) — a net buyer of y. p_y rises, he moves to (9,11). Then:
explain: At (9,11) he still consumes more y than his endowment 10, so he stays a net buyer of y; a net buyer facing a higher price of that good is worse off.
a: Still a net buyer of y, so he must be worse off.

q: At current prices the consumer neither buys nor sells (stays at her endowment). Which can happen?
explain: Starting exactly at the endowment, a rise in px steepens the line through ω and makes good x more valuable to sell, so she may become a net seller of x.
a: If the price of x rises, she might start SELLING good x.

q: Consumer is a net seller of x (consumes less x than her endowment). Which is correct?
explain: For a net seller of x a fall in px lowers the price she receives (worse off); the gross-demand response splits into a substitution effect (raises x) and an endowment/income effect whose sign depends on whether x is normal or inferior, so more than one listed statement is correct.
a: More of these are correct (about how normal/inferior x reacts to its own price fall).

q: The net demand for good 1 is defined as:
explain: Net demand is what she ends up consuming minus what she started with: x₁ minus ω₁, positive for a net buyer and negative for a net seller.

q: In the endowment model, gross demand for good 1 is:
explain: Gross demand is the total consumed, x₁; net demand is gross demand minus the endowment, x₁ minus ω₁.
opts: the total amount x₁ she finally consumes
only the extra units she buys in the market

q: A consumer owns ω₁=10 units of good 1 and optimally consumes x₁=6. She is:
explain: Net demand = x₁ minus ω₁ = 6 minus 10 = minus 4, so she sells 4 units of good 1.
opts: a net seller of 4 units of good 1
a net buyer of 4 units of good 1

q: A consumer with endowment ω₁=7 is a net buyer of 5 units of good 1. Her gross demand (total consumption) of good 1 is:
explain: Gross demand = endowment plus net purchases = 7 plus 5 = 12.

q: Endowment ω=(10,5), prices p₁=2, p₂=4. Selling her whole endowment, the most of good 1 she could consume is:
explain: Endowment value = 2·10 plus 4·5 = 40; spent entirely on good 1 at p₁=2 that buys 40/2 = 20 units.

q: Same data (ω=(10,5), p₁=2, p₂=4). The most of good 2 she could consume is:
explain: Endowment value 40 spent entirely on good 2 at p₂=4 buys 40/4 = 10 units.

q: Endowment ω=(20,10), prices p₁=3, p₂=4. The money value of her endowment (her budget) is:
explain: Endowment income = p₁ω₁ plus p₂ω₂ = 3·20 plus 4·10 = 60 plus 40 = 100.

q: Preferences u=x₁x₂, endowment ω=(4,8), prices p₁=2, p₂=4. Her net demand for good 1 is:
explain: Income = 2·4 plus 4·8 = 40; Cobb-Douglas u=x₁x₂ sets x₁*=40/(2·2)=10, so net demand = 10 minus 4 = 6, a net buyer.

q: Same setup (u=x₁x₂, ω=(4,8), p₁=2, p₂=4). Her net demand for good 2 is:
explain: x₂*=40/(2·4)=5, so net demand = 5 minus 8 = minus 3: she sells 3 units of good 2, financing her 6 extra units of good 1 (2·6 = 4·3).

q: In that example she is a net buyer of good 1 (buys 6), so for good 2 she must be:
explain: With two goods the budget through ω forces buying one good on net to be paid for by selling the other, so she is a net seller of good 2.
opts: also a net buyer of good 2

q: Preferences u=x₁x₂, endowment ω=(4,8), p₂=4 fixed. As p₁ rises she switches from net buyer to net seller of good 1 exactly when p₁ reaches:
explain: She is at her endowment for good 1 when x₁*=ω₁: (4p₁ plus 32)/(2p₁)=4 gives p₁=8; above 8 she consumes less than ω₁ and becomes a net seller.

q: Prices p₁=2, p₂=3. A consumer owns 6 units of good 1 and B units of good 2. Her net demand for good 1 is 3 and her gross demand for good 2 is 8. Then B equals:
explain: x₁*=6 plus 3 = 9 and y*=8. The budget through the endowment 2·9 plus 3·8 = 2·6 plus 3·B gives B = 10.

q: Preferences u=min(x₁,x₂), endowment ω=(12,3), prices p₁=1, p₂=2. Her optimal consumption of each good is:
explain: Perfect complements sit on x₁=x₂; the budget 1·x₁ plus 2·x₂ = 1·12 plus 2·3 = 18 with x₁=x₂ gives (1 plus 2)x = 18, so x = 6.

q: In that problem (u=min(x₁,x₂), ω=(12,3), optimum 6 of each) she is:
explain: She consumes 6 of good 1 (less than 12, sells 6) and 6 of good 2 (more than 3, buys 3): a net seller of good 1 and a net buyer of good 2, with values matching (1·6 = 2·3).
opts: a net seller of good 1 and a net buyer of good 2

q: Preferences u=x₁ plus x₂ (perfect substitutes), endowment ω=(10,10), p₁=1, p₂=2. Her optimal consumption of good 1 is:
explain: Since p₁ is below p₂ and the goods are equally liked, she holds only the cheaper good 1; selling all good 2 gives x₁ = (1·10 plus 2·10)/1 = 30.

q: In the endowment Slutsky equation the income term is (ω₁ minus x₁)·∂x₁/∂m. For a consumer with ω₁=10 and x₁=6, the coefficient (ω₁ minus x₁) equals:
explain: ω₁ minus x₁ = 10 minus 6 = 4, positive because she consumes less than she owns (a net seller of good 1).

q: For a net buyer with ω₁=6 and x₁=10, the endowment-Slutsky coefficient (ω₁ minus x₁) is:
explain: ω₁ minus x₁ = 6 minus 10 = minus 4, negative because a net buyer consumes more than she owns.

q: In the endowment model the Slutsky equation splits ∂x₁/∂p₁ into three parts. They are:
explain: With an endowment the total effect = ordinary substitution effect + ordinary income effect + the extra endowment-income effect, because the value of the endowment moves with p₁.
opts: the substitution effect, the ordinary income effect, and the endowment-income effect
only a substitution effect and an income effect
two substitution effects and one income effect
a substitution effect and a supply effect

q: A net seller of a normal good sees its own price rise. Combining a negative substitution effect with a positive endowment-income effect, the total effect on her gross demand for that good is:
explain: For a net seller (ω₁ minus x₁ greater than 0) of a normal good the endowment-income term is positive and opposes the negative substitution term, so the sign is ambiguous: this is what makes backward-bending labour supply possible.
opts: ambiguous in sign (the two effects oppose each other)

q: After a price change, a consumer's ORIGINAL optimal bundle is still affordable at the new prices. Compared with before, she is:
explain: She could still buy her old bundle, so her new optimum is at least as good: a revealed-preference argument, making her weakly better off.
opts: at least as well off (weakly better)

q: At prices (p₁,p₂)=(2,4) with endowment (10,10) she chose (4,13). Then p₁ rises to 4 (p₂ still 4). Her old bundle (4,13) is:
explain: New income = 4·10 plus 4·10 = 80; the old bundle now costs 4·4 plus 4·13 = 68, at most 80, so it is still (strictly) affordable.
opts: still affordable (it costs 68, at most the new income 80)
affordable only if p₂ also falls
exactly on the new budget line

q: Same consumer: at (2,4) with endowment (10,10) she chose (4,13), a net seller of good 1; then p₁ rises to 4. She becomes:
explain: She sells good 1 (4 less than 10); a net seller is made better off when the price of the good she sells rises, so her welfare rises.
opts: better off (a net seller when the price she receives rises)

q: Preferences u=x₁x₂, endowment ω=(4,2). At p₁=2, p₂=4 she consumes exactly her endowment. If p₁ rises to 3 (p₂=4), her consumption of good 1 becomes:
explain: New income = 3·4 plus 4·2 = 20; x₁*=20/(2·3)=10/3, about 3.33, below ω₁=4, so the price rise turned her into a net seller of good 1.
opts: 10/3, about 3.33, so she is now a net seller of good 1

q: A consumer who currently neither buys nor sells (she consumes exactly her endowment). A rise in p₁ will, in general, make her:
explain: At the endowment her indifference curve is tangent to the old line; a steeper line (higher p₁) through ω moves her optimum to less good 1, so she starts selling good 1.

q: A consumer is a net seller of good 1 when her gross demand x₁ is:
explain: Selling on net means consuming less than owned: x₁ less than ω₁.

q: The quantity p₁ω₁+p₂ω₂ (the market value of what the consumer owns) is her:
