explain: It is the endowment's market value, which serves as her money income in the budget p₁x₁+p₂x₂ = p₁ω₁+p₂ω₂.
opts: endowment income (the budget she can spend)

q: With p₁=6 and p₂=2, selling one unit of good 1 lets the consumer buy how many units of good 2?
explain: One unit of good 1 is worth p₁=6; at p₂=2 that buys 6/2 = 3 units of good 2.

q: Endowment ω=(8,6), prices p₁=5, p₂=10. The horizontal intercept of the budget line (all wealth on good 1) is at x₁ =
explain: Endowment value = 5·8 plus 10·6 = 100; all spent on good 1 at p₁=5 gives x₁ = 100/5 = 20.

q: Bruno the dog is given either 4 bones and 2 chews, or 2 bones and 4 chews. If a bone and a chew have the same price, the two gifts give Bruno:
explain: At equal prices both endowments have the same value (4 plus 2 = 2 plus 4 = 6 units' worth), and the budget line depends only on prices and endowment value, so it is identical.
opts: the same budget line (equal total value)
budget lines that cross only at the origin

q: A commuter grows vegetables (good 2) and buys petrol (good 1) to drive to work, buying far more petrol than she could ever sell. A rise in the petrol price makes her:
explain: She is a net buyer of good 1 (petrol); a net buyer is made worse off when the price of the good she buys rises.
opts: worse off (she is a net buyer of petrol)

q: Prices are unchanged, but a consumer's endowment is replaced by a different bundle worth MORE at those prices. For her budget line this is:
explain: With prices fixed only the endowment's value matters; a higher value shifts the line out in parallel (same price ratio, more income).
opts: a pure parallel outward shift (higher income, same slope)
a pivot around the old endowment

q: Endowment ω=(3,9), prices p₁=4, p₂=2. She chooses (6,3). The value she spends buying good 1 equals the value she raises selling good 2, namely:
explain: Net purchase of good 1 = 3 units, worth p₁·3 = 12; net sale of good 2 = 6 units, worth p₂·6 = 12; equal, so (6,3) lies on the budget line through ω.
opts: 12 = 12 (buys 3 of good 1 worth 12, sells 6 of good 2 worth 12)

q: A net seller has ω₁=12, x₁=8, ∂x₁/∂m=0.5 (a normal good), and an own-substitution effect equal to minus 1. The endowment Slutsky total ∂x₁/∂p₁ = (substitution) + (ω₁ minus x₁)·∂x₁/∂m equals:
explain: (ω₁ minus x₁)·∂x₁/∂m = (12 minus 8)·0.5 = 2; total = minus 1 plus 2 = 1, positive, so gross demand rises with its own price: the backward-bending mechanism for a net seller.
opts: 1 (positive: demand rises with its own price)

q: In the labour-leisure model, the two goods the consumer chooses between are:
explain: The consumer trades off leisure against consumption; hours worked are the leftover time, not a separate choice good.

q: Hours worked L, leisure R, and the time endowment T are related by:
explain: All available time is either worked or enjoyed as leisure, so L = T minus R.

q: Rearranged, the budget line C=w(T-R)+m<sub>0</sub> reads:
explain: C = w(T minus R)+m0 = (m0+wT) minus wR, a line in R with intercept m0+wT and slope minus w.

q: In this budget line, the wage w is best described as:
explain: Each hour of leisure costs the wage forgone, so w is the price of leisure.

q: The slope dC/dR of the labour-leisure budget line equals:
explain: From C = (m0+wT) minus wR the slope dC/dR is minus w.

q: The bundle (R=T, C=m<sub>0</sub>) on this line is the point where the consumer:
explain: At R=T she uses all time as leisure and works zero hours, consuming only m0.
opts: takes all time as leisure and works zero hours

q: Working every available hour (R=0) gives consumption equal to:
explain: Working every hour (R=0) gives C = m0 + wT.

q: With T=10, w=1, m<sub>0</sub>=2, consumption at leisure R=6 equals:
explain: C = m0 + w(T minus R) = 2 + 1*(10 minus 6) = 6.

q: In that same example, hours worked at R=6 are:
explain: Hours worked L = T minus R = 10 minus 6 = 4.

q: At an interior labour-leisure optimum, the consumer's marginal rate of substitution between leisure and consumption equals:
explain: At an interior optimum the indifference curve is tangent to the budget line, so MRS = w.

q: Holding T and m<sub>0</sub> fixed, a wage increase makes the budget line:
explain: A higher wage raises the price of leisure, steepening the line while it still passes through the endowment point, so it pivots and steepens.
opts: steeper, pivoting at the fixed endowment point
flatter, pivoting at the fixed endowment point

q: Mock-exam Q9 setup: C and R (leisure) are both normal goods, and the total time endowment rises. The new optimal consumption C<sub>1</sub><sup>*</sup> compared with the old C<sub>0</sub><sup>*</sup> is:
explain: With C and R both normal a bigger time endowment (a pure income gain) raises both, so C1* exceeds C0*.

q: The reason a bigger time endowment raises BOTH leisure and consumption is that it:
explain: A larger T raises full income m0+wT at an unchanged wage (price of leisure), a pure income effect on two normal goods, raising both.
opts: raises full income at an unchanged price ratio, a pure income effect on two normal goods
has no effect on the budget line

q: When only T rises (w and m<sub>0</sub> fixed), the relative price of leisure, the wage w:
explain: Raising T does not change the wage, so the price of leisure is unchanged.

q: Because the relative price does not change when T rises, the effect on demand is:
explain: Because the wage (relative price of leisure) is unchanged, only an income effect operates when T rises.
opts: split evenly between substitution and income effects

q: If leisure were an inferior good instead of normal, a bigger time endowment would make optimal leisure R<sub>1</sub><sup>*</sup>:
explain: If leisure were inferior, the pure income gain from a bigger T would lower leisure.

q: If leisure were inferior and R<sub>1</sub><sup>*</sup> fell as in the previous question, hours worked would:
explain: If R1* falls then L = T minus R rises: hours worked increase.

q: If consumption C were (hypothetically) an inferior good, a bigger time endowment would make C<sub>1</sub><sup>*</sup>:
explain: If consumption were inferior, the income gain from a bigger T would lower C.

q: Numerically: budget C=10-R (smaller endowment, T<sub>0</sub>=10) has optimum E<sub>0</sub>=(R,C)=(4,6); budget C=14-R (bigger endowment, T<sub>1</sub>=14) has optimum E<sub>1</sub>=(6,8). Leisure R rose from 4 to:
explain: Reading the optima, leisure R rose from 4 to 6.

q: In that same pair of optima, consumption C rose from 6 to:
explain: Reading the optima, consumption C rose from 6 to 8.

q: Using T<sub>0</sub>=10, T<sub>1</sub>=14, R<sub>0</sub>=4, R<sub>1</sub>=6, hours worked L=T-R went from 6 to:
explain: L = T minus R: L0 = 10 minus 4 = 6 and L1 = 14 minus 6 = 8.

q: The single word in the exam question that pins the answer down to “higher” rather than “ambiguous” is:
explain: Only the word 'normal' rules out the inferior case and pins the answer to 'higher' rather than 'ambiguous'.

q: A wage increase makes leisure relatively more expensive. The substitution effect alone therefore pushes the consumer toward:
explain: A wage rise makes leisure relatively dearer, so the substitution effect alone cuts leisure and raises hours.

q: The same wage increase also makes the worker richer (higher full income). If leisure is normal, the income effect alone pushes toward:
explain: A wage rise raises full income; with leisure normal the income effect alone raises leisure and cuts hours.

q: Because the substitution and income effects of a wage change point in opposite directions for leisure, the net effect of a wage rise on hours worked is:
explain: For leisure the substitution effect (cut) and income effect (raise) conflict, so the net effect of a wage rise on hours is ambiguous.

q: This ambiguity is the standard explanation for why an individual's labour-supply curve (wage on the vertical axis, hours on the horizontal) can:
explain: Because the two effects conflict, hours can fall as the wage rises, giving a backward-bending supply curve.

q: At relatively low wages, typically in these models, labour supply tends to be:
explain: At low wages the substitution effect usually dominates, so labour supply slopes up.

q: At high wages, the segment of the curve where hours FALL as the wage rises further reflects:
explain: Where hours fall as the wage rises further, the income effect has come to dominate the substitution effect.
opts: the income effect dominating the substitution effect

q: A rise in non-labour (unearned) income m<sub>0</sub>, holding the wage fixed, changes the relative price of leisure:
explain: A change in m0 leaves the wage (price of leisure) unchanged, so there is no substitution effect.
opts: not at all; there is no substitution effect

q: With leisure a normal good, a rise in non-labour income m<sub>0</sub> alone (wage fixed) makes hours worked:
explain: A rise in m0 is a pure income effect; with leisure normal it raises leisure and cuts hours worked.

q: Compared with a wage change, a change in non-labour income m<sub>0</sub> is:
explain: A change in non-labour income leaves the wage unchanged, so it is a pure income effect.
opts: equally ambiguous, also has a substitution effect
unambiguous, a pure income effect only

q: A lottery winner who suddenly receives a large lump sum of non-labour income, with leisure normal, is predicted by this model to work:
explain: A lottery win is a pure rise in m0; with leisure normal the income effect makes her work fewer hours.

q: Alice: wage 6/h, 70 h/week, child allowance 40, wage taxed 10%. Maximum weekly consumption? [40 + 0.9·6·70]
explain: Maximum consumption uses all 70 hours: m0 + (1 minus t)*w*T = 40 + 0.9*6*70 = 40 + 378 = 418.

q: Molly: u=CR, 16 h/day, no non-labour income, wage 3/h, needs 20/day, welfare = (needs−earnings) if she works ≥6 h. Daily welfare received?
explain: Welfare tops consumption up to needs (20) when she works at least 6h, so C=20 for any hours >=6; to maximise u=CR she works the minimum 6h, earns 3*6=18, and receives welfare 20 minus 18 = 2. (u=200 beats the no-welfare optimum u=192.)

q: Lisa: u=C(2+R), 200 h/month, no non-labour income, wage 4/h, welfare 200 if she doesn't work. Hours she works?
explain: Working, u=C(2+R)=4(200 minus R)(2+R) is maximised at R=99, so L=200 minus 99=101 (u=40804 beats the not-working u=40400).

q: Henry: 25 h/week for leisure+work, allowance 110, wage 5/h, spends 175 on consumption. Relaxation hours? [C=110+5(25−R)=175 ⇒ 25−R=13]
explain: C = 110 + 5*(25 minus R) = 175 gives 25 minus R = 13, so relaxation time R = 12.

q: Leisure is a normal good; fixed total time between work and leisure. Which is true?
explain: Correction: with leisure a NORMAL good a bigger time endowment is a pure rise in full income at an unchanged price of leisure, so the demand for leisure RISES (it would fall only if leisure were inferior). The original key stated the inferior-good result, so the answer is corrected here.
a: An increase in the total time available raises the demand for leisure (a pure income effect, since leisure is normal); it would fall only if leisure were inferior.

q: Bill and Donald: same well-behaved prefs, leisure normal, no non-labour income, same time budget, Bill has the higher wage. Then:
explain: With no non-labour income both budget lines pass through (R=T, C=0), and the higher-wage line is steeper, so for consumption both the substitution and income effects of the higher wage point up: Donald (lower wage) always consumes less, though hours are ambiguous. (Consumption is taken to be normal, as usual.)
a: Donald might work more or less than Bill, but he will always consume less.

q: An income-tax rate on earnings rises. Total tax payments always increase if:
explain: Revenue is t·w·L. If leisure demand rises with the after-tax wage, labour supply falls with the wage (backward-bending). A higher tax rate lowers the after-tax wage, so leisure falls and hours rise; both the rate and hours rise, so revenue always increases.
a: The consumer's demand for leisure is increasing in the real wage.

q: The real wage rises. Which is true?
explain: A worker is a net seller of leisure; when the price of leisure (the wage) rises, her old bundle stays affordable, so by revealed preference anyone who already worked is at least as well off, in fact strictly better.
a: A consumer who already worked before the change always becomes better off.

q: Willy: wage 5/h, 100 h/week, a 100 grant, 50% tax on labour income, u=CR. Hours he chooses to work? [after-tax wage 2.5]
explain: After-tax wage = 0.5*5 = 2.5; full income = 100 + 2.5*100 = 350; u=CR spends half on leisure, so R = 175/2.5 = 70 and hours L = 100 minus 70 = 30.

q: John: u=CR, time endowment T=100 h, non-labour income m₀=50, after-tax wage w=2.5. His optimal consumption C is:
explain: Full income = m₀ plus wT = 50 plus 2.5·100 = 300; with u=CR he spends half on consumption, so C = 300/2 = 150.

q: Same John (u=CR, T=100, m₀=50, w=2.5). His optimal leisure R and hours worked L are:
explain: Leisure R = full income/(2w) = 300/(2·2.5) = 60, so hours worked L = T minus R = 100 minus 60 = 40.

q: A worker earns wage 10/h, works up to 40 h, has non-labour income 50, and pays a 20% tax on labour income. Her maximum weekly consumption is:
explain: Take-home wage = 0.8·10 = 8; working all 40 h gives 8·40 = 320, plus non-labour income 50 = 370.

q: A person's reservation wage is:
explain: Below the reservation wage she supplies zero hours; at it she is indifferent between working and staying at the no-work point (R=T, C=m₀).
opts: the wage at which she is just indifferent between working and not working
the highest wage any employer will pay

q: Preferences u=CR, time endowment T=120, non-labour income m₀=60. Her reservation wage (below which she works zero hours) is:
explain: The reservation wage equals the MRS at the no-work point (R=T, C=m₀): MRS = C/R = m₀/T = 60/120 = 0.5.

q: Preferences u=CR, T=80, non-labour income m₀=40. She is offered a wage of 0.4/h. She will:
explain: Reservation wage = m₀/T = 40/80 = 0.5; the offered 0.4 is below it, so she supplies zero hours.
opts: not work (0.4 is below her reservation wage of 0.5)

q: A worker is paid w for the first H hours and a higher wage w' (greater than w) for hours beyond H. In the leisure-consumption diagram her budget line has:
explain: Below the kink (working more than H, i.e. less leisure) each hour earns the higher w', so that segment is steeper; the premium creates a convex kink at R = T minus H.
opts: a kink, steeper in magnitude in the overtime region (less leisure)
no kink, a single straight line
a kink but flatter in the overtime region

q: First 8 hours are paid 10/h, overtime beyond 8 h is paid 15/h, no non-labour income. Working 10 hours gives consumption:
explain: First 8 h: 8·10 = 80; 2 overtime hours: 2·15 = 30; total 110.

q: Same overtime scheme (10/h up to 8 h, 15/h beyond, no non-labour income). Working exactly 8 hours gives consumption:
explain: Eight hours at the base wage: 8·10 = 80 (no overtime yet).

q: Preferences u=CR, T=100, wage w=2. Non-labour income rises from 0 to 40. Optimal leisure changes by:
explain: R = full income/(2w); at m₀=0, R = 200/4 = 50; at m₀=40, R = 240/4 = 60; leisure rises by 10 (a pure income effect, leisure normal).

q: Same change (u=CR, T=100, w=2, m₀ from 0 to 40). Hours worked change by:
explain: Hours L = T minus R fall from 50 to 40 as leisure rises, i.e. by minus 10: more unearned income means less work when leisure is normal.

q: Preferences u=CR, m₀=0, T=100. When the wage rises from 4 to 8, optimal hours worked change by:
explain: With m₀=0 and u=CR, R = wT/(2w) = T/2 = 50 for any wage, so hours L = 50 regardless: the substitution and income effects on leisure exactly cancel.

q: Preferences u=CR, m₀=40, T=100. When the wage rises from 4 to 8, optimal hours worked change by:
explain: R = (m₀ plus wT)/(2w): at w=4, R=(40 plus 400)/8=55, L=45; at w=8, R=(40 plus 800)/16=52.5, L=47.5; hours rise by 2.5 because the fixed m₀ weakens the income effect so substitution dominates.

q: With a proportional tax t on labour income, the interior labour-leisure optimum sets the marginal rate of substitution of leisure for consumption equal to:
explain: The price of leisure is the take-home wage w(1 minus t), so tangency requires MRS = w(1 minus t).
opts: the after-tax wage w(1 minus t)

q: For u=CR the MRS of leisure for consumption is C/R. At an optimum with after-tax wage 3 and leisure R=40, consumption C is:
explain: The optimum sets C/R = after-tax wage = 3, so C = 3·40 = 120.

q: A higher labour-income tax lowers the take-home wage. For a worker on the upward-sloping part of the labour-supply curve, hours worked will:
explain: On the upward-sloping (substitution-dominant) range, a lower after-tax wage reduces hours worked.

q: In C = m₀ + w(1 minus t)(T minus R), the term w(1 minus t) represents:
explain: Each hour of leisure costs the wage forgone after tax, w(1 minus t).
opts: the take-home (after-tax) wage, the price of leisure

q: With m₀=20, wage w=10, tax t=0.2, time endowment T=50, the worker's full income (value of all time worked plus m₀) is:
explain: Full income = m₀ plus w(1 minus t)T = 20 plus 0.8·10·50 = 20 plus 400 = 420.

q: If the wage on offer is below a person's reservation wage, she chooses to work:
explain: Below the reservation wage the no-work corner (R=T, C=m₀) is best, so she supplies zero hours.
opts: more as the wage falls further

q: Preferences u=CR, m₀=0, wage w=2. The time endowment rises from T=100 to T=120. Optimal leisure changes by:
explain: R = wT/(2w) = T/2, so R rises from 50 to 60 as T rises: a pure income effect, since the wage (price of leisure) is unchanged.

q: An individual labour-supply curve bends backward over a range precisely when, there, leisure is:
explain: A wage rise's substitution effect cuts leisure while its income effect (leisure normal) raises it; backward bending occurs when the income effect dominates.
opts: a normal good whose income effect outweighs the substitution effect

q: Two people have identical preferences and the same wage, but Ann has higher non-labour income than Ben. With leisure normal, Ann works:
explain: Higher unearned income is a pure income effect; with leisure normal it raises leisure and lowers hours, so Ann works less.

q: Holding preferences and the time endowment fixed, a person with higher non-labour income m₀ has a reservation wage that is:
explain: The reservation wage equals MRS at (R=T, C=m₀); for u=CR that is m₀/T, which rises with m₀, so richer non-labour income makes work less tempting.
opts: higher (she needs a bigger wage to start working)

q: At wage 4 a worker chooses 40 hours; at wage 6 she chooses 36 hours; at wage 8 she chooses 30 hours. Over the range shown her labour supply is:
explain: Hours fall (40, 36, 30) as the wage rises, so the income effect dominates and the supply curve bends backward.
opts: backward bending (hours fall as the wage rises)

q: Gross wage 20/h; the labour-income tax falls from 40% to 25%. The take-home wage rises from:
explain: After-tax wage = w(1 minus t): 20·0.6 = 12 at t=0.4, and 20·0.75 = 15 at t=0.25.

q: A student has a scholarship of 100/week (non-labour income) and can tutor at 15/h after tax. If she tutors 12 hours, her weekly consumption is:
explain: Consumption = m₀ plus after-tax wage·hours = 100 plus 15·12 = 100 plus 180 = 280.

q: A wage rise raises the price of leisure. Decomposed, its substitution effect on HOURS is ___ and (with leisure normal) its income effect on HOURS is ___:
explain: Substitution: dearer leisure means less leisure and more hours (positive). Income (leisure normal): richer means more leisure and fewer hours (negative). They conflict, so net hours are ambiguous.

q: The time constraint splits the endowment T into:
explain: All available time is either leisure or work: T = R + L.
opts: leisure R and labour L, with T = R + L

q: In the labour-leisure model, the opportunity cost (price) of one hour of leisure is:
explain: Taking an hour of leisure means giving up the wage from working it, so the wage is the price of leisure.
opts: the wage that hour would have earned

q: Compared with a wage change, a change in non-labour income m₀ (wage fixed) is:
explain: m₀ shifts the budget in parallel without changing the wage, so leisure's relative price is unchanged: only an income effect operates.
opts: a pure income effect (no change in the price of leisure)

q: Preferences u = C + 8·ln(R) (quasilinear in consumption), time endowment T=24, after-tax wage w=2. Optimal leisure R is:
explain: MRS = (8/R)/1 = 8/R; setting it equal to the wage 2 gives R = 8/2 = 4 (quasilinear preferences make leisure depend only on the wage).

q: Same quasilinear worker (u = C + 8·ln R, T=24). When the after-tax wage rises from 2 to 4, optimal hours worked change from:
explain: R = 8/w falls from 4 to 2 as the wage rises, so hours L = 24 minus R rise from 20 to 22; with no income effect on leisure only the substitution effect operates (always more hours).
opts: 20 to 22 (hours rise; quasilinear leisure has no income effect)

q: For a gamble with outcomes x<sub>i</sub> and probabilities p<sub>i</sub>, the expected value EV equals:
explain: Expected value is the probability-weighted sum of outcomes, EV = Σ pᵢxᵢ. Option B states exactly this; u(Σ pᵢxᵢ) is u(EV) and Σ pᵢu(xᵢ) is expected utility.
opts: the utility of the average outcome, u(Σ p<sub>i</sub> x<sub>i</sub>)

q: Expected utility EU of the same gamble equals:
explain: Expected utility weights the utility of each outcome by its probability, EU = Σ pᵢu(xᵢ). Σ pᵢxᵢ is EV and u(EV) is the utility of the mean.
opts: the utility of the smallest x<sub>i</sub>

q: The certainty equivalent CE of a gamble is defined by:
explain: The certainty equivalent is the sure amount whose utility equals the gamble's expected utility: u(CE) = EU.

q: In plain words, the certainty equivalent is:

q: The risk premium RP of a gamble is defined as:

q: The certainty equivalent of receiving a sure amount of 80 (no risk at all) is:

q: An agent must choose between gamble A (certainty equivalent 120) and gamble B (certainty equivalent 110). A utility-maximizer will:

q: In the homeowner example (wealth 100, loss 84 with probability 0.5, u(w) = √w), the maximum willingness to pay for full insurance (51) exceeds the actuarially fair premium (42) by exactly:

q: The present-value form of the intertemporal budget line is:

q: The relative price of one extra unit of future consumption, measured in present consumption given up, equals:

q: If r rises, the relative price of future consumption:

q: The future value of the endowment, FV, equals:

q: When the interest rate r rises, a saver's future consumption c<sub>2</sub>:

q: When r rises, a saver's present consumption c<sub>1</sub>:

explain: Exact Fisher: 1 + real = 1.10/1.05 = 1.047619, so real ≈ 4.76% (not the approximate 5%).

q: A saver (lender) faces a fall in the interest rate. She is:

worse off, because present consumption is dearer

q: A consumer who is a borrower sees the interest rate rise and remains a borrower. Compared with before, he is:
explain: A borrower buys present consumption; a higher r raises its price, so a borrower who stays a borrower is worse off.

q: A consumer optimally chooses to consume exactly her endowment (c₁ = m₁, c₂ = m₂). If the interest rate changes, she is:
explain: The endowment point lies on the budget line at every r, so it stays affordable; she can do no worse and may find a newly affordable preferred bundle, hence weakly better off.

q: When the interest rate r rises, the present value of a fixed future endowment m₂:
explain: PV of the future endowment is m₂/(1+r), which decreases as r rises.

q: Your nominal income and all prices both rise by exactly 10%. Your real purchasing power:
explain: Real purchasing power is nominal income divided by the price level; if both rise 10% the ratio is unchanged.

q: Nominal income doubles (rises 100%) while all prices triple (rise 200%). Real purchasing power:
explain: Real income scales by 2/3 (≈ 0.667), which is below 1, so purchasing power falls.

explain: Real factor = 1.05/1.02 = 1.0294, so real income rises about 2.94% (not the approximate 3%).

q: With c₁ horizontal and c₂ vertical and r = 25%, the magnitude of the slope of the intertemporal budget line is:
explain: The slope is −(1+r) = −1.25, so its magnitude is 1.25.

q: Holding the endowment (m₁,m₂) fixed with m₂ greater than 0, an increase in r causes the present value of the endowment to:
explain: PV = m₁ + m₂/(1+r); raising r shrinks the discounted future term, so PV falls.

q: In the two-period model, the price of one unit of present consumption c₁ measured in units of future consumption c₂ given up is:
explain: Giving up one unit of c₁ today and saving it yields (1+r) units of c₂, so the relative price of present consumption is 1+r.

q: A student earns nothing this year and 11000 next year, and can borrow at r = 10%. The most she can consume this year by borrowing against next year's income is:
explain: Maximum c₁ is the present value of the endowment: 0 + 11000/1.1 = 10000.

q: The problem `min p· x s.t. u(x)=u<sub>0</sub>' is expenditure minimisation; it defines:
explain: Minimising cost to reach a fixed utility (EMP) yields Hicksian (compensated) demand.

q: What does the Marshallian (Walrasian) demand x(p,m) hold fixed as price varies?
explain: Marshallian demand holds money income m (and other prices) fixed.
opts: the quantity of the other good

q: What does the Hicksian (compensated) demand h(p,u) hold fixed as price varies?
explain: Hicksian demand holds the utility level u fixed.
opts: the price of the other good only

q: A fall in p<sub>1</sub> traced along the Marshallian demand curve shows:
explain: The Marshallian curve embeds both effects, so it traces the total (substitution plus income) effect.

nothing, since income is not held fixed

q: A fall in p<sub>1</sub> traced along the Hicksian demand curve shows:
explain: The Hicksian curve holds utility fixed, so it isolates the pure substitution effect.

the change in income needed to restore the old bundle

q: Which demand curve can, in the rare Giffen case, slope upward in its own price?
explain: Only Marshallian demand can slope up (the Giffen case); Hicksian demand always slopes down.

q: Which demand curve is guaranteed to slope downward in its own price, for any good, with no exceptions?
explain: Hicksian demand obeys the compensated law of demand and slopes down for every good.

q: Plugging the Marshallian demand x(p,m) back into u(x) gives:
explain: Substituting Marshallian demand into utility yields the indirect utility function v(p,m).

q: The minimised value of p· x in the expenditure-minimisation problem defines:
explain: The minimised cost in the EMP is the expenditure function e(p,u).

q: Roy's identity recovers which function from the indirect utility function v(p,m)?
explain: Roy's identity recovers Marshallian demand from v(p,m).

q: Roy's identity states that x<sub>i</sub>(p,m) equals:
explain: Roy's identity: x_i = −(∂v/∂p_i)/(∂v/∂m).
opts: (∂ v/∂ p<sub>i</sub>)/(∂ v/∂ m), with no minus sign
the ratio of two Hicksian demands

q: Shephard's lemma recovers which function from the expenditure function e(p,u)?
explain: Shephard's lemma recovers Hicksian demand from e(p,u).

q: Shephard's lemma states that h<sub>i</sub>(p,u) equals:
explain: Shephard's lemma: h_i = ∂e/∂p_i.

just one derivative of e, with no ratio and no minus sign

q: The identity e(p,v(p,m))= ____ \ says that reaching the utility your income m already buys costs exactly:

q: The identity v(p,e(p,u))= ____ \ says that maximising utility with just enough income to reach u gets you back to:
explain: v(p, e(p,u)) = u: maximising utility with just enough income to reach u returns u.

q: Which identity turns Hicksian demand into Marshallian demand?
explain: x(p,m) = h(p, v(p,m)) evaluates Hicksian demand at u = v(p,m) to give Marshallian demand.

q: Which identity turns Marshallian demand into Hicksian demand?
explain: h(p,u) = x(p, e(p,u)) evaluates Marshallian demand at m = e(p,u) to give Hicksian demand.

q: The Slutsky equation writes the total price effect ∂ x<sub>i</sub>/∂ p<sub>j</sub> as:
explain: Slutsky: ∂x_i/∂p_j = ∂h_i/∂p_j − x_j·(∂x_i/∂m), the substitution term minus an income term.
opts: the substitution effect minus x<sub>j</sub> times the income-derivative of Marshallian demand
the income effect minus the substitution effect
the substitution effect plus the income effect, always with the same sign
just the substitution effect, since income is irrelevant

q: In the Slutsky equation, the term -x<sub>j</sub>·(∂ x<sub>i</sub>/∂ m) is called:
explain: The term −x_j·(∂x_i/∂m) is the income term of the Slutsky equation.

q: The expenditure function e(p,u), as a function of prices p, is:
explain: The expenditure function is concave in prices.

q: The indirect utility function v(p,m), as a function of prices p, is:
explain: The indirect utility function is quasiconvex in prices.

q: e(p,u) is increasing in u and homogeneous of which degree in prices p?
explain: e(p,u) is increasing in u and homogeneous of degree one in prices.

q: v(p,m) is homogeneous of which degree in (p,m) jointly?
explain: Scaling all prices and income together leaves choices unchanged, so v is homogeneous of degree zero in (p,m).

q: A Giffen good requires:

q: Laurie has 3 useless CDs (no player). U=x+f(y)z<sup>2</sup>, z=3, f(y)=0 if y<1 else 6. Most she will pay for a CD player? [f jumps 0→6: gain=6·3²=54]

q: Which statement about Equivalent Variation (EV) after a tax increase is true?

q: Claire: quasilinear, inverse demand p=24−4x, currently buys 5 units. Consumer surplus? [½·base·height, choke price 24, but at x=5 p=4 … area of triangle above price to demand]

q: Consumer surplus computed under the WALRASIAN demand, where richer people buy LESS of x (inferior). If price rises, the calculated CS loss is:

q: Walrasian demand for x is steeper than the Hicksian (price vertical). Then:

q: The two central optimisation problems of consumer duality are:
explain: Consumer duality pairs the utility-maximisation problem (UMP) with the expenditure-minimisation problem (EMP).

explain: UMP yields Marshallian demand; EMP yields Hicksian demand.

q: Which chain correctly recovers Marshallian demand from the expenditure side of duality?

q: Because e(p,u) is concave in prices, its own second derivative ∂²e/∂p_i² is ___, which is exactly the statement that ∂h_i/∂p_i is ___.
explain: Concavity of e makes ∂²e/∂p_i² ≤ 0; since h_i = ∂e/∂p_i, this is ∂h_i/∂p_i ≤ 0, the downward-sloping compensated demand.

q: Marshallian and Hicksian demand for a good coincide exactly at the price where:

q: Demand slopes downward mainly because:

opts: each extra unit is worth less to the buyer than the last one

q: A price change's welfare effect on the consumer is approximated by:

q: Bruno pays a lot (in enthusiasm) for his first treat and barely reacts to his fifth. This is:

q: If the price of a good falls and nothing else changes, Marshallian consumer surplus:

q: Ordinary consumer surplus is measured under:
explain: Plain consumer surplus is the area under the Marshallian (ordinary, actual) demand curve; CV and EV use the two Hicksian curves.

q: Your surplus on a single unit bought at price p is:

q: For a price DECREASE, the compensating variation CV is:
explain: A price fall benefits the consumer, so holding her at the original u₀ requires taking money away: CV is negative for a price decrease.
opts: negative (income could be taken from the consumer and leave her at the original utility)

q: The income offer curve (income expansion path) is:
opts: the set of optimal bundles traced out as income changes, with prices held fixed
the set of optimal bundles as the price of one good changes
the locus where MRS is undefined
explain: Hold prices fixed and raise income: the budget line shifts out parallel and the optimum moves. Joining those optima in good-x/good-y space gives the income offer curve (also called the income expansion path).

q: An Engel curve plots:
opts: the quantity demanded of one good against income (prices fixed)
quantity demanded against that good's own price
good y against good x along the budget line
explain: The Engel curve reads one good's demand as a function of income. It is derived from the income offer curve by tracking a single good's quantity as income rises.

q: For Cobb-Douglas preferences u = x^a y^b, the Engel curve for good x is:
opts: a straight line through the origin
explain: Cobb-Douglas demand is x = (a/(a+b))·m/px, which is linear in m with zero intercept: doubling income doubles x. So the Engel curve is a ray from the origin (income elasticity exactly 1).

q: If good x is a normal good, its Engel curve:
explain: Normal means demand rises with income, so the Engel curve slopes upward. Inferior goods are the exception (demand falls with income over some range).

q: Good x is inferior over some income range. Over that range the Engel curve:
opts: bends back / slopes negatively (x falls as income rises)
must be a ray through the origin
explain: Inferior means the income effect on demand is negative: as income rises the consumer buys less x, so the Engel curve slopes the 'wrong' way over that range (classic examples: bus rides, instant noodles as income grows).

q: For homothetic preferences (Cobb-Douglas, perfect substitutes, perfect complements all qualify), the income offer curve is:
opts: a straight-line ray through the origin, and every good's income elasticity is 1
a curve that never passes through the origin
explain: Homothetic preferences scale demands proportionally with income: budget shares stay constant, income elasticities all equal 1, and the optima line up on a ray from the origin. Cobb-Douglas is the leading case.

q: Classify goods by income elasticity of demand (eta). Which is correct?
opts: luxury eta > 1, necessity 0 < eta < 1, inferior eta < 0
luxury eta < 0, necessity eta > 1, inferior eta = 0
luxury eta = 1, necessity eta = 1, inferior eta = 1
luxury eta = 0, necessity eta < 0, inferior eta > 1
explain: eta = (dx/dm)(m/x). eta > 1 means the budget share rises with income (luxury); 0 < eta < 1 means the share falls but quantity still rises (necessity); eta < 0 means quantity falls (inferior). Cobb-Douglas sits exactly on the borderline eta = 1.

q: For quasilinear preferences u = v(x) + y (with y the linear good), the Engel curve for good x is:
opts: vertical: x is (near) constant as income rises, so extra income goes to y
explain: The interior optimum solves v'(x) = px/py, which has no m in it, so x does not depend on income above a threshold. The Engel curve for x is vertical (income elasticity 0); all extra income is spent on the linear good y.

q: For perfect complements u = min(ax, by), the income offer curve is:
opts: the ray y = (a/b)x through the origin
a curve bending toward the y-axis
explain: The optimum always sits at the corner where ax = by, i.e. y = (a/b)x, whatever the income. As income rises the corner slides out along that ray, so the income offer curve is exactly the ray y = (a/b)x (perfect complements are homothetic).

q: The income offer curve and the Engel curve differ in that:
opts: the income offer curve lives in good-x/good-y space; the Engel curve plots one good's quantity against income
they are the same picture with different labels
the Engel curve lives in good-x/good-y space; the income offer curve plots quantity against income
both are drawn in price/quantity space
explain: The income offer curve joins the optimal (x, y) bundles as income changes. Reading off good x's quantity at each income and re-plotting quantity-against-income gives the Engel curve.

q: Compare the income offer curve (income changes) with the price offer curve (one price changes). Which statement is right?
opts: income offer curve: budget line shifts out parallel; price offer curve: budget line pivots about an intercept
both trace optima as the same price changes
income offer curve: budget pivots; price offer curve: budget shifts parallel
explain: Raising income shifts the budget line out parallel (prices fixed) and the income offer curve joins those optima. Changing one price pivots the budget line about the other good's intercept, and the price offer curve (from which the ordinary demand curve is read) joins those optima instead.

q: u = x·y (so a = b = 1) with px = 2. Writing the Engel curve x as a function of income m, what is its slope dx/dm?
explain: Cobb-Douglas: x = (a/(a+b))·m/px = (1/2)·m/2 = m/4. As a function of m this is a straight line through the origin with slope 1/4 = 0.25.

q: For any Cobb-Douglas good, what is the income elasticity of demand?
explain: x = (a/(a+b))·m/px is proportional to m, so eta = (dx/dm)(m/x) = 1 exactly. This is why Cobb-Douglas goods are neither luxuries nor necessities: the budget share a/(a+b) never changes with income.

q: u = x^(1/3) y^(2/3), px = 5. At income m = 300 the consumer buys x = 20. Income rises to m = 600. How many units of x now?
explain: The x share is a/(a+b) = 1/3, so px·x = m/3, i.e. x = m/(3·px) = m/15. The Engel curve is linear through the origin, so doubling income from 300 to 600 doubles x: 20 -> 40 (x = 600/15 = 40).

q: Quasilinear u = 2·sqrt(x) + y with py = 1 and px = 1/2. What quantity of x does the consumer buy (for income high enough to be interior), and note it does not change with income?
explain: MRS = MUx/MUy = (1/sqrt(x))/1 = px/py = 1/2, so sqrt(x) = 2 and x = 4. There is no m in this condition: x stays at 4 as income rises (income elasticity 0, vertical Engel curve); every extra crown goes to y.

q: Optimum condition: state it and say when it fails.
a: Tangency $\text{MRS}=\dfrac{MU_1}{MU_2}=\dfrac{p_1}{p_2}$ (equal marginal utility per crown). Fails at corners (perfect substitutes), kinks (Leontief), and non-convex preferences.

q: Compensating variation: definition and sign for a price rise.
a: Money at the NEW prices to restore the OLD utility: $CV=e(p^1,u^0)-m$. For a price rise $CV>0$ (a loss).

q: A saver's interest rate falls: effect on $c_1,c_2$ and welfare?
a: Future gets dearer. SE: $c_1\uparrow,c_2\downarrow$. IE (lender, poorer): both $\downarrow$. So $c_2$ falls, $c_1$ ambiguous; she is worse off.

q: Define the MRS and why it diminishes under convexity.
a: $\text{MRS}=MU_x/MU_y=$ |slope of the IC|, the $y$ given up for one more $x$. It falls as $x$ rises: that bowing-in IS convexity.

q: Convexity of preferences: definition and effect on the optimum.
a: A mix of two indifferent bundles is at least as good (upper-contour sets convex). Strict convexity $\Rightarrow$ a unique optimum.

q: What does it mean that utility is ordinal?
a: Only the ranking matters. Any strictly increasing transform $g(u)$ gives the same preferences, MRS and demand; a decreasing one reverses them.

q: Marshallian vs Hicksian demand: what is fixed, when do they coincide?
a: Marshallian $x(p,m)$ fixes income (has the income effect); Hicksian $h(p,u)$ fixes utility (pure substitution). They meet at $x(p,e(p,u))=h(p,u)$.

q: State the Slutsky equation and the sign of each part (normal good, $p_i$ up).
a: $\dfrac{\partial x_i}{\partial p_i}=\dfrac{\partial h_i}{\partial p_i}-x_i\dfrac{\partial x_i}{\partial m}$. SE $\le 0$; income term also negative for a normal good, so demand falls.

q: Classify a price rise into normal / inferior / Giffen.
a: SE always lowers $x$. Normal: IE reinforces ($x\downarrow$). Inferior: IE opposes but SE wins ($x\downarrow$). Giffen: IE dominates ($x\uparrow$). Giffen $\subset$ inferior.

q: Why is Hicksian demand always downward-sloping but Marshallian not?
a: $\dfrac{\partial h_i}{\partial p_i}=\dfrac{\partial^2 e}{\partial p_i^2}\le 0$ ($e$ concave in $p$). Marshallian adds the income effect, which for a Giffen good tips the total positive.

q: Define own-price, income and cross-price elasticity.
a: $\varepsilon=\dfrac{dQ}{dP}\dfrac{P}{Q}$, $\eta=\dfrac{dQ}{dm}\dfrac{m}{Q}$, $\varepsilon_{ij}=\dfrac{dQ_i}{dP_j}\dfrac{P_j}{Q_i}$. $|\varepsilon|>1$ elastic; $\eta>1$ luxury; $\varepsilon_{ij}>0$ substitutes.

q: What is a Giffen good and why must it be inferior?
a: Demand rises when its own price rises. It is strongly inferior with a large budget share, so the negative income effect outweighs the substitution effect; inferiority is necessary.

q: State WARP and how you test it on data.
a: If $A$ is revealed preferred to $B$ ($p^A\!\cdot B\le p^A\!\cdot A$), then $B$ is never revealed preferred to $A$. Violation: two bundles each affordable when the other was chosen.

q: State Roy's identity and Shephard's lemma.
a: $x_i=-\dfrac{\partial v/\partial p_i}{\partial v/\partial m}$ (Marshallian from $v$); $h_i=\dfrac{\partial e}{\partial p_i}$ (Hicksian from $e$).

q: Explain the duality of UMP and EMP.
a: Two views of one optimum. $v$ and $e$ are inverses: $e(p,v(p,m))=m$, $v(p,e(p,u))=u$; and $x(p,e(p,u))=h(p,u)$.

q: Key properties of the expenditure function $e(p,u)$.
a: Increasing in $p$ and $u$, homogeneous degree 1 in $p$, concave in $p$; $\dfrac{\partial e}{\partial p_i}=h_i$ and $\dfrac{\partial h_i}{\partial p_i}\le 0$.

q: Define equivalent variation and its ordering with CV and $\Delta CS$.
a: $EV=m-e(p^0,u^1)$. For a price rise (magnitudes) $CV>|\Delta CS|>EV$; reversed for a fall; all equal if quasilinear.

q: What does consumer surplus measure, and when is it exact?
a: Area under inverse demand above price, $CS=\int_0^{Q^*}(p(Q)-p^*)\,dQ$. Exact (=CV=EV) only with no income effect, i.e. quasilinear preferences.

q: Laspeyres vs Paasche: definitions and the cost-of-living bias.
a: Laspeyres $\dfrac{\sum p^1 q^0}{\sum p^0 q^0}$ overstates; Paasche $\dfrac{\sum p^1 q^1}{\sum p^0 q^1}$ understates. True index lies between.

q: Define quasilinear preferences and why $CV=\Delta CS=EV$.
a: $u=v(x)+y$: $x$ solves $v'(x)=p_x/p_y$, independent of income. No income effect, so Marshallian $=$ Hicksian and the three measures coincide.

q: Why is a net seller of a good better off when its price rises?
a: The budget passes through the endowment; a higher $p_1$ raises its value and the old bundle stays affordable with slack, so a net seller reaches a higher IC.

q: Labour-leisure optimum and the backward-bending region.
a: $\text{MRS}_{C,R}=w(1-t)$. A wage rise: SE toward work, IE toward leisure; if IE dominates, hours fall as $w$ rises (backward-bending).

q: Define the certainty equivalent and risk premium; why full insurance at fair odds?
a: $u(CE)=EU$, $RP=EV-CE>0$ (concave $u$). A fair premium equals the expected loss, so full cover gives a sure $EV$; a risk-averter prefers that to the gamble.

q: Section C. A good x is sold at a quantity discount: a higher price per unit up to some quantity, then cheaper above it. Draw the budget line (x horizontal, other good y) and locate the optimum. What is special about the budget set?

explain: For full marks: correct intercepts; a kink at the threshold quantity; the steeper segment below and flatter above; note the budget set is non-convex; the optimum at a tangency on one segment or at the kink.

q: Section C. The price of good x falls. On an indifference-curve diagram decompose the total effect into the substitution and income effects (Slutsky), labelling the three bundles.
a: Old optimum A; pivot the budget to the new slope keeping A affordable (compensated budget); its optimum B is the substitution effect (A→B); restoring full income gives C, the income effect (B→C).
explain: For full marks: original budget and optimum A; new (flatter) budget; a compensated budget parallel to the new one through A; substitution effect A→B along it; income effect B→C to the new optimum; SE always toward the cheaper good.

q: Section C. For a price rise of good x, show the compensating variation and the equivalent variation on an indifference-curve diagram, and say which utility level each uses.
a: CV = extra income at the NEW prices to get back to the OLD utility u0; EV = income at the OLD prices equivalent to the loss, referenced to the NEW utility u1.
explain: For full marks: old and new budget lines and the two indifference curves u0>u1; CV measured at new prices restoring u0; EV measured at old prices reaching u1; state the ordering CV > |ΔCS| > EV for a rise.

q: Section C. Draw the two-period budget constraint through an endowment (m1,m2), mark the saver and borrower regions and an optimum. What is the slope?
a: The line runs through the endowment with slope −(1+r); left of it (c1<m1) she saves/lends, right of it she borrows; the optimum is where MRS = 1+r.
explain: For full marks: line through the endowment; slope −(1+r); saver region to the left, borrower to the right; tangency optimum with MRS = 1+r; PV and FV are the two intercepts.

q: Section C. Illustrate risk aversion: on a graph of a concave utility of wealth, show expected utility, the certainty equivalent, and the risk premium.
a: Draw u(w) concave; the gamble's EU sits on the chord between the two states at wealth EV; u(EV) on the curve is higher; CE is the wealth where the curve reaches EU, and RP = EV − CE.
explain: For full marks: concave u(w); the two state wealths and the chord between them; EU on the chord above EV; u(EV) on the curve; CE read off to the left of EV; the horizontal gap EV−CE labelled as the risk premium.

q: Section C. Using an endowment (buying-and-selling) diagram, show why a net seller of a good is better off when its price rises.
a: The budget passes through the endowment; a higher p1 pivots it steeper about the endowment; the old bundle stays affordable with slack, so the net seller reaches a higher indifference curve.
explain: For full marks: budget through the endowment point; a rise in p1 pivots it about the endowment (steeper); the endowment still affordable; the new optimum on a higher IC for a net seller (a net buyer would be worse off).

q: Section C. Draw indifference curves for perfect complements u=min(ax,by) with a budget line, and find the optimum. Where does it lie?
a: L-shaped indifference curves with corners on the ray ax=by; the optimum is at that corner, where ax=by meets the budget.
explain: For full marks: L-shaped curves; corners along the ray ax=by; the budget line; optimum at the intersection of ax=by and the budget (never a tangency).

q: Section C. Draw indifference curves for perfect substitutes u=ax+by with a budget line, and find the optimum. When is it a corner and when is it any point?
a: Straight parallel indifference curves with slope −a/b; the optimum is a corner (all on the good with the higher MU per crown) unless the budget has the same slope, when any point is optimal.
explain: For full marks: straight parallel ICs of slope −a/b; the budget of slope −px/py; corner solution on the good with higher MU/price; the tie case a/b = px/py giving a whole segment.

q: Section C. One good is an economic bad. Draw the indifference curves and the optimum. Which way do the curves slope and where is the best point?
a: With y a bad the curves slope upward (more of the good x is needed to offset more of the bad y); the optimum sets y=0 and spends everything on the good.
explain: For full marks: upward-sloping indifference curves; the direction of increasing utility (toward more x, less y); the budget line; optimum at the corner y=0, x=m/px.

q: Section C. On a demand diagram show the consumer surplus at a price, and the change in consumer surplus when the price falls.
a: CS is the area under the demand curve above the price; a price fall adds the area between the two price lines under demand.
explain: For full marks: demand curve; price line; CS as the triangle above the price and below demand; the extra CS when the price falls as the region between the two prices; label the axes.

q: Section C. Draw the labour-leisure budget and the optimum, and illustrate a backward-bending response to a wage rise.
a: Budget from the time endowment with slope −w(1−t), optimum where MRS = w(1−t); a wage rise pivots it steeper, and if the optimum moves to MORE leisure the income effect dominates (hours fall).
explain: For full marks: leisure on the horizontal axis; budget from (T, m0) with slope −w(1−t); tangency optimum MRS=w(1−t); a steeper budget after a wage rise; the new optimum at more leisure, so hours fall (backward-bending).

q: Section C. Income rises while prices stay fixed. Draw the income offer curve (income expansion path) in good-x/good-y space, then derive the Engel curve for good x. What shape does each take for Cobb-Douglas (homothetic) preferences, and how would an inferior good differ?
a: Shift the budget line out parallel as income rises and join the tangency optima: that is the income offer curve. For Cobb-Douglas it is a ray through the origin, so the Engel curve (quantity of x against income) is a straight line through the origin. An inferior good's Engel curve bends back (negative slope) over the inferior range.
explain: For full marks: parallel outward budget shifts (prices fixed, no pivot); tangency optima joined into the income offer curve; note it is a ray through the origin for homothetic/Cobb-Douglas preferences (constant budget shares, income elasticity 1); derive the Engel curve by plotting good x's quantity against income; upward-sloping (straight through the origin for CD) for a normal good, bending back for an inferior good.
